bio.en: Krithika Shankarraman was the first marketing hire and VP of Marketing at OpenAI, the first marketing hire at Stripe, and an early marketing leader at Retool, Dropbox, and Android at Google; she is now an Executive in Residence at Thrive Capital advising founders on marketing.
bio.zh: Krithika Shankarraman 是 OpenAI 的首位市场负责人兼市场副总裁、Stripe 的首位市场负责人，也是 Retool、Dropbox 以及 Google Android 的早期市场领袖；她目前是 Thrive Capital 的驻场高管（Executive in Residence），为创始人提供市场方面的顾问支持。

summary.en: Krithika argues that while playbooks and frameworks exist for everything, real marketing still requires putting in the hours to deeply understand your customer rather than blindly copying what others do. Drawing on her time as the first marketing hire at OpenAI and Stripe, she explains that even for a product as magical as ChatGPT, marketing's job is to create 'use-case epiphany'—helping people realize what the product is actually for. She shares a four-step diagnostic approach to marketing, an 'anti-playbook playbook,' and what B2B companies can learn from consumer marketing. The episode also covers career advice for aspiring marketers and the essential marketing literacy that every non-marketer needs to build successful products.
summary.zh: Krithika 认为，尽管到处都有现成的打法和框架，但真正的市场营销仍然需要投入大量时间去深度理解你的客户，而不是盲目照搬别人的做法。结合她在 OpenAI 和 Stripe 担任首位市场负责人的经历，她解释说，即便像 ChatGPT 这样神奇的产品，市场营销的工作也是创造“用例顿悟”——帮助人们想清楚这个产品到底能用来做什么。她分享了一套四步诊断式的营销方法、一个“反套路手册”，以及 B2B 公司能从消费级营销中学到什么。这一期还涵盖了给有志于做市场的人的职业建议，以及每个非市场人员都需要具备、才能做出成功产品的市场常识。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you were an early and the first marketing hire at some of the most iconic companies in the world. turns.zh: 因此，您是世界上一些最具标志性的公司的早期也是第一位营销人员。我今天想通过我们的聊天基本上了解一下您曾经工作过的许多公司，看看我们可以从您在这些公司领导营销的时间中汲取哪些经验教训。我想从 OpenAI 开始。没什么大不了的。您是 OpenAI 的第一位营销人员。那里的事情似乎进展得很顺利。我相信 ChatGPT 是历史上增长最快的产品。这引起共鸣吗？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: It does. Not that I can take credit for it.
turns.zh: 确实如此。这并不是说我可以因此而获得功劳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, we'll talk about that. Either way, nice job. Let me ask you this. A lot of people might be hearing like, "Oh, ChatGPT." It's like, why do you need marketing? It's like the most magical thing in the history of the world. How much value does anything add to making it as successful? Can you just talk about just the value that a marketing person adds to a product like that that's already incredible?
turns.zh: 好吧，我们会讨论这个。不管怎样，干得好。让我问你这个。很多人可能会听到“哦，ChatGPT”。就像，为什么需要营销？这就像世界历史上最神奇的事情。任何事情能够为其成功增加多少价值？您能谈谈营销人员为这样的产品添加的价值吗？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah. When you think about all of the different stages of the funnel, awareness was clearly not the problem that ChatGPT or OpenAI had. Everyone knew of ChatGPT, but when you clicked one zoom level further, the thing that came up was, "I don't know what to use it for. I don't know what it replaces. Should I be using search for this? Should I be using ChatGPT for this? How can it even help me?" And so the work of marketing ended up becoming, creating this sort of use case epiphany where people could say, "I had no idea ChatGPT can do that. And yeah, maybe I should be using it for X, Y, Z reason in my own life." And so I think you have to be very diagnostic in terms of what can marketing be doing to help, rather than just going off of the typical top of funnel, and then middle of funnel and conversion-oriented tactics that end up being in a playbook.
turns.zh: 是的。当你考虑漏斗的所有不同阶段时，意识显然不是 ChatGPT 或 OpenAI 遇到的问题。每个人都知道 ChatGPT，但是当您进一步单击一个缩放级别时，出现的问题是，“我不知道用它做什么。我不知道它取代什么。我应该使用搜索来实现这个吗？我应该使用 ChatGPT 来实现这个吗？它对我有何帮助？”因此，营销工作最终变成了创建这种用例顿悟，人们可以说，“我不知道 ChatGPT 可以做到这一点。是的，也许我应该在自己的生活中出于 X、Y、Z 的原因使用它。”因此，我认为你必须非常善于诊断营销可以提供哪些帮助，而不是仅仅脱离典型的漏斗顶部，然后是漏斗中间和最终出现​​在剧本中的以转化为导向的策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So for folks that listen to this podcast, it's a lot of product managers, product builders. A lot of them don't have a lot of experience with marketing. I think it's an important insight there of just, this is a thing marketing can help you with is helping people understand how to use your product, understand use cases, understand examples, things like that. So I think as we go through this, I think this is useful for folks to understand of, here's what you may not be good at and may need marketing help with.
turns.zh: 所以对于听这个播客的人来说，有很多产品经理、产品构建者。他们中的许多人没有丰富的营销经验。我认为这是一个重要的见解，营销可以帮助你帮助人们了解如何使用你的产品，了解用例，理解示例，诸如此类。所以我认为，当我们经历这个过程时，我认为这对人们理解很有用，这是你可能不擅长并且可能需要营销帮助的内容。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah. When done right, product management and product marketing should be best friends, right? And you are working together at every stage of product development. Rather than thinking of it as a handoff at the end of the conveyor belt when the product's been built, you sort of hand it off to marketing to take it out the door. If you can think of it as sort of a three-legged race from the very beginning of product development, then you go to market with the right thing in the first place. You get these insights from customers, you hear the language that they're using, which can be the sort of cheat code for how to message and position the product in market. And of course, there's a creativity angle on how to differentiate your product in the market, but ideally, you're doing that in lockstep with the product management side.
turns.zh: 是的。如果做得好，产品管理和产品营销应该是最好的朋友，对吧？你们在产品开发的每个阶段都在共同努力。您不要将其视为产品制造完成后在传送带末端的交接，而是将其交给营销人员以将其带出大门。如果您从产品开发一开始就可以将其视为三足竞赛，那么您首先就将正确的产品推向市场。您可以从客户那里获得这些见解，您可以听到他们使用的语言，这可能是一种如何在市场上传达信息和定位产品的作弊代码。当然，如何让你的产品在市场上脱颖而出，有一个创造性的角度，但理想情况下，你要与产品管理方面保持同步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other element of ChatGPT's marketing success, I know that you spent a lot of time on the enterprise side, is just consumerish marketing tactics for enterprisey products. Can you just talk about that? And it feels like that's emerging more and more just like consumer tactics for enterprise products.
turns.zh: ChatGPT 营销成功的另一个要素，我知道您在企业方面花了很多时间，就是针对企业产品的消费者营销策略。你能简单谈谈吗？感觉这越来越像企业产品的消费者策略。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: In typical organizations that I've been a part of and leading marketing for, the enterprise side of the house, the B2B side of the house usually fits the mold of demand generation where you're creating demand for the sales team and you're bringing new customers and prospects into the fold and into the orbit of the company. That again, was not the problem at OpenAI. When we turned on the contact sales form for ChatGPT Enterprise, which was one of my first launches at the company, our lead volume 40 X-ed overnight. It was unanticipated even beyond our wildest expectations. And so some of the things that I had to do are not typical to marketing at all. I sat down with ChatGPT and I coded up a Python script that ended up functioning as our first lead qualification, lead-scoring model. That was used in production for way too long, longer than I'd care to admit.
turns.zh: 在我参与并领导营销的典型组织中，企业方面、B2B 方面通常符合需求生成的模式，在这种模式中，您为销售团队创造需求，并将新客户和潜在客户带入公司并进入公司轨道。这又不是 OpenAI 的问题。当我们打开 ChatGPT Enterprise 的联系销售表单（这是我在公司首次推出的产品之一）时，我们的潜在客户数量一夜之间增加了 40 倍。这是出乎我们意料之外的，甚至超出了我们最疯狂的预期。因此，我必须做的一些事情对于营销来说根本不是典型的。我与 ChatGPT 坐下来，编写了一个 Python 脚本，最终成为我们的第一个潜在客户资格、潜在客户评分模型。它在生产中使用的时间太长了，比我愿意承认的时间还要长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny. I think about when ChatGPT first launched and OpenAI just launched, everyone was just like, "How will you make money? How do you make money with something like this chatbot that's pretty smart, but sort of not that smart?" I remember there's a video of Sam Altman being asked, "How do you make money with something like this?" And I don't know if you just saw this, he just like, "At some point we will ask ChatGPT, how do we make money?"
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。我想，当 ChatGPT 首次推出和 OpenAI 刚刚推出时，每个人都在想，“你将如何赚钱？你如何通过像这个非常聪明但又不太聪明的聊天机器人这样的东西赚钱？”我记得有一段视频萨姆·奥尔特曼被问到：“你如何用这样的东西赚钱？”我不知道你是否刚刚看到这个，他只是说，“在某个时候我们会问 ChatGPT，我们如何赚钱？”

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yes. And I think the reality is it's not a solved problem. And a lot of folks, a lot of companies in the AI domain are trying to figure out the right pricing model. And it's something that you've talked about in your newsletter and so on, but there is a value creation aspect to using AI that doesn't kind of neatly fit the mold of SaaS-based pricing or seed-based pricing, or even usage-based pricing. So, I think there are still some frontiers to figuring out where is the value, how do different types of organizations and companies and consumers find value? And again, it's not the typical sort of KPIs that you would typically try to optimize and maximize.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为现实是这不是一个已解决的问题。人工智能领域的很多人、很多公司都在试图找出正确的定价模型。这是您在时事通讯等中谈到的内容，但使用人工智能有一个价值创造方面，这并不完全符合基于 SaaS 的定价或基于种子的定价，甚至基于使用的定价的模式。所以，我认为弄清楚价值在哪里，不同类型的组织和公司以及消费者如何找到价值，仍然有一些前沿？再说一遍，这不是您通常会尝试优化和最大化的典型 KPI。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I will say, though, in terms of pricing, it feels like ChatGP, it works. It's just like a monthly fee, talk to it up to a certain limit. It's wild to think back now, there was a sense, "We don't have no idea how will this make money." Now it seems so obvious.
turns.zh: 不过，我想说的是，就定价而言，感觉就像 ChatGP，它很有效。就好像月费一样，到一定限度就可以了。现在回想起来真是疯狂，有一种感觉，“我们不知道这将如何赚钱。”现在看来是那么明显。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Truly was a research preview.
turns.zh: 确实是一个研究预览。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I remember Sam Altman just launched, "Here, check out this chat thing that we are trying with," and then the fastest product growth in history. No big deal. I want to come back to this point you made about this playbook, anti-playbook kind of a thinking. You kind of pointed out that with ChatGPT and OpenAI, there was no playbook, and you find that often people following playbooks don't work. Talk about that insight.
turns.zh: 我记得 Sam Altman 刚刚推出，“在这里，看看我们正在尝试的这个聊天工具”，然后是历史上最快的产品增长。没什么大不了的。我想回到你对这个剧本、反剧本的思考的观点。您有点指出，对于 ChatGPT 和 OpenAI，没有剧本，而且您发现遵循剧本的人通常不起作用。谈谈这个见解。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: In my current role in my career, I've spoken with a lot of founders, and typically, the founders reach out because I've worked at companies that they look up to and they're looking for that playbook. They're looking for, "Hey, just tell me how Stripe did it. Tell me how Retool did it. Tell me how OpenAI did it." And I really hesitate to share any such detail because there was a combination of context, competitive landscape, and the overall sort of zeitgeist of when the company's operating, how the company's operating, that really adds a lot of nuance to what works in the market. (00:10:43): And so doing the same things, like if you're just kind of copying the outcomes or the outputs of the strategy and trying to follow in the footsteps of the tactics, you're not paying enough attention to the inputs and, what were the variables and the deciding factors which led to that strategy in the first place? So what I like to do is try to unpack more of a framework for how do you get to become more of a diagnostician to understand the right strategy or tactic in the first place, rather than saying, "How do you copy something that led someone else to success?" Because those criteria may not apply to you at all.
turns.zh: 在我目前的职业生涯中，我与很多创始人进行过交谈，通常，创始人会主动联系我，因为我曾在他们尊敬的公司工作过，并且他们正在寻找该剧本。他们正在寻找，“嘿，告诉我 Stripe 是如何做到的。告诉我 Retool 是如何做到的。告诉我 OpenAI 是如何做到的。”我真的很犹豫是否要分享任何此类细节，因为背景、竞争格局以及公司何时运营、公司如何运营的整体时代精神结合在一起，这确实给市场上的运作方式增加了很多细微差别。 (00:10:43)：所以做同样的事情，比如如果你只是复制策略的结果或输出并试图追随策​​略的脚步，那么你就没有对输入给予足够的关注，以及，首先导致该策略的变量和决定因素是什么？因此，我喜欢做的就是尝试解开更多的框架，让你如何成为一名诊断专家，首先了解正确的战略或策略，而不是说“你如何复制那些导致别人成功的东西？”因为这些标准可能根本不适用于您。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's follow that thread because everyone's like, "Goddamn, I need a play. Just tell me how to do this." Okay, so there's no playbooks that you... If your advice is, "Don't just copy what other companies do that have done well," what should people be doing? How do they approach figuring out how to market their product and help it grow faster?
turns.zh: 所以让我们遵循这个思路，因为每个人都会说，“天哪，我需要一场比赛。告诉我该怎么做吧。”好吧，所以你没有任何剧本……如果你的建议是，“不要只是复制其他公司做得很好的做法”，那么人们应该做什么？他们如何弄清楚如何营销他们的产品并帮助其更快增长？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah. So I was an engineer before I became a marketer, and so I have brought a little bit of an engineer's framework to the marketing side of the house. And so something that I've tried to do is put together a four-step process that has served me pretty well. The first step here is diagnosing. So, diagnosing the actual problem. Again, this usually means taking a zoom back when a founder comes and asks, "Hey, we really need to hire a demand gen leader. Who do you know in your network that we should be thinking about?" And I'm like, "Let's talk about your funnel. Do you have a lot of people coming in at the top of the funnel? And when they do come in at the top of the funnel and you start talking to them and having a sales conversation, how likely is it that you close them? How likely is it that you win that deal?" (00:12:20): That usually tells you very astutely, do you have product market fit? Once you're already in the room and people are converting, you have found that problem statement that is critical to them that is hurting them the most, and your solution is resonating as a solve to that problem. And so that means yes, probably throwing in more at the top of the funnel is a very good move to make at that time. But on the other hand, if you say, "Yeah. I mean, we get a lot of interest, but once they're in the room, they have a bunch of questions. They're asking about, how do you compare to X competitor and Y competitor? And why does it cost so much?" and et cetera, et cetera. (00:12:59): That probably means that there's more to be done in the product market fit zone rather than throwing in more at the top of the funnel because you have a leaky funnel at the bottom. And so hiring a demand generator may be the worst thing that you can do versus thinking about more of a product marketer who's thinking about the competitive differentiation, the positioning, the sales enablement that gets more people through at the bottom. So that's that diagnostic step at the top. (00:13:24): Second to me is analyzing your competitors' approaches. So to me, this is not about being super laser focused on your competition because that leads to these local maxima rather than thinking about face shift changes and breakthroughs that you can make as a company. But when you analyze your competitors' approaches, evaluating what others do in the space can kind of give you a useful baseline and identify opportunities and gaps and niches that your company can take in instead. (00:13:51): And then, this is the critical step. The next one is you have to intentionally take a different path than what everyone else is doing. And so driving a strategy that sort of sets the company apart is really critically important. I think it's so core to the discipline of marketing, ensuring that differentiation in the market. And you don't have to go into a cave to come up with these ideas and strategies. You can usually go and look at domains that are far outside of your own rather than your direct competitors and come up with some great ideas that you can cross apply and bring in and steal into your own domain or vertical instead. (00:14:28): And then the final piece is just experiment, test, validate all of that, and then scale what works and kind of discard what doesn't. So you really have to have a lot of that ability to throw away work when you might have spent a ton of calories on this wonderful piece of content. But if it's not working, don't double down on it. That bias of the sunk cause fallacy really comes into play, especially when you've poured your heart and soul into creating artifacts for marketing. So experiment, test, validate. Give people that psychological safety to fail, especially your teams and organizations. And then, yeah, once you find what works, really double down on it.
turns.zh: 是的。因此，在成为营销人员之前，我是一名工程师，因此我将一些工程师的框架引入了营销方面。因此，我尝试做的事情就是整合一个四步流程，这对我来说非常有用。这里的第一步是诊断。因此，诊断实际问题。同样，这通常意味着当创始人过来询问“嘿，我们真的需要聘请一位需求生成领导者。你知道在你的网络中我们应该考虑谁？”时，我们需要回顾一下。我想，“让我们谈谈你的漏斗。你有很多人进入漏斗的顶部吗？当他们确实进入漏斗的顶部时，你开始与他们交谈并进行销售对话，你关闭他们的可能性有多大？你赢得那笔交易的可能性有多大？” (00:12:20)：这通常会非常敏锐地告诉你，你的产品适合市场吗？一旦你已经进入房间并且人们正在转换，你就会发现对他们来说至关重要的问题陈述对他们造成的伤害最大，并且你的解决方案作为该问题的解决方案引起了共鸣。所以这意味着是的，在漏斗顶部投入更多资金可能是当时非常好的举措。但另一方面，如果你说，“是的。我的意思是，我们得到了很多兴趣，但是一旦他们进入房间，他们就会提出很多问题。他们会问，你与 X 竞争对手和 Y 竞争对手相比如何？为什么要花这么多钱？”等等，等等。 (00:12:59)：这可能意味着在产品市场适合区域还有更多工作要做，而不是在漏斗顶部投入更多，因为漏斗底部有漏洞。因此，雇佣需求生成者可能是你能做的最糟糕的事情，而不是更多地考虑产品营销人员，产品营销人员正在考虑竞争差异化、定位、销售支持，从而让更多的人在底层度过难关。这就是顶部的诊断步骤。 (00:13:24)：对我来说第二个是分析竞争对手的方法。所以对我来说，这并不是要过度关注你的竞争对手，因为这会导致这些局部最大值，而不是考虑你作为一家公司可以实现的面貌转变和突破。但是，当您分析竞争对手的方法时，评估其他人在该领域所做的事情可以为您提供有用的基线，并确定您的公司可以利用的机会、差距和利基市场。 (00:13:51)：然后，这是关键的一步。下一个是你必须有意识地走一条与其他人不同的道路。因此，推动一项使公司脱颖而出的战略确实至关重要。我认为这是营销学科的核心，确保市场的差异化。而且你不必进入洞穴才能想出这些想法和策略。您通常可以去看看那些远离您自己的领域而不是您的直接竞争对手的领域，并提出一些可以交叉应用、引入和窃取到您自己的领域或垂直领域的好主意。 (00:14:28)：最后的部分就是实验、测试、验证所有这些，然后衡量有效的内容并丢弃无效的内容。因此，当您可能在这段精彩的内容上花费了大量卡路里时，您确实必须拥有大量扔掉工作的能力。但如果它不起作用，就不要加倍努力。这种沉没原因谬误的偏见确实发挥了作用，尤其是当你全心全意地创造营销产品时。所以实验、测试、验证。给予人们失败的心理安全感，尤其是你的团队和组织。然后，是的，一旦你找到了有效的方法，就真的要加倍努力。

So essentially if you think you're like, "I need help with marketing," or, "I have a problem and I think I need to hire a demand gen person or a paid growth person or a SEO person, or I don't know, content writer," something like that, before you do that, first of all, go through these four steps. (00:15:24): So step one is diagnose. Spend time understanding what's the specific problem you want to solve, then analyze. This is so interesting, I've never heard it this way. So then it's analyze what your competition is doing so that you can then, one, find inspiration and see where gaps exist. And then it sounds like the core part of it is just make sure you differentiate and choose a different path versus just try to be the better thing or the cheaper thing. And then the final piece is just like, "Okay, here's our path. Let's test run some small scale tests to see if this would work."
turns.zh: 让我总结一下您刚才在这里分享的内容。因此，本质上，如果您认为自己是这样的，“我需要营销方面的帮助”，或者“我遇到了问题，我认为我需要雇用一名需求生成人员或付费增长人员或搜索引擎优化人员，或者我不知道，内容作家”，类似的事情，在您这样做之前，首先，请完成这四个步骤。 (00:15:24)：第一步是诊断。花时间了解您想要解决的具体问题是什么，然后进行分析。这太有趣了，我从来没有听说过这样的说法。因此，接下来就是分析你的竞争对手在做什么，这样你就可以，第一，找到灵感并看看存在差距。听起来它的核心部分就是确保你与众不同并选择不同的路径，而不是仅仅尝试成为更好的东西或更便宜的东西。然后最后一部分就像是，“好吧，这就是我们的路径。让我们进行一些小规模的测试，看看这是否可行。”

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah. I'm a marketer through and through now. So I mean you got diagnose, D. Analyze, A. Take a different path, T. And experiment for the E. So it's the DATE framework. I've just kind of coined it.
turns.zh: 是的。我现在是一名彻头彻尾的营销人员。所以我的意思是你得到了诊断，D.分析，A.采取不同的路径，T.并为E进行实验。所以这是DATE框架。我只是创造了它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, beautiful. Okay. We got a new framework hot off the presses. I love it. DATE, okay. So with differentiation, what's your thoughts on saying you're just a lot better or a lot cheaper?
turns.zh: 哦，美丽。好的。我们得到了一个刚刚印刷出来的新框架。我喜欢它。日期，好的。那么，对于差异化，您对于说自己更好还是更便宜有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Being cheaper is a race to the bottom, especially when you think about sort of scaling laws and how things are playing out. Every company is sort of becoming an AI company at this time. And so as models get cheaper and more capable, being cheaper is not going to be the thing that really is a durable approach in the market. And I think in terms of doing things differently, it's not just for the sake of it. I think it's really that novelty and that differentiation is something that people are craving for. They're not looking for yet another tool in the market. They are looking for something that aligns with their values, aligns with what their goals are. And so if you can be really crisp on understanding the user need, understanding what is the problem space in which they're operating, I think that one-two punch of a fantastic product experience, and then the marketing experience to match, can be a superpower for your company.
turns.zh: 变得更便宜是一场逐底竞争，尤其是当你考虑某种规模法则以及事情如何发展时。此时每家公司都在某种程度上成为人工智能公司。因此，随着模型变得更便宜、功能更强大，更便宜的价格将不会成为市场上真正持久的方法。我认为以不同的方式做事不仅仅是为了这样做。我认为这确实是人们所渴望的新颖性和差异化。他们并不是在市场上寻找另一种工具。他们正在寻找符合他们价值观、符合他们目标的东西。因此，如果您能够真正清晰地了解用户需求，了解他们所面临的问题空间，我认为一击二打的出色产品体验，以及与之相匹配的营销体验，可以成为您公司的超能力。

turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。因此，让我们看一下您曾经工作过的公司的示例，然后这可能会将我们带到您在故事中工作过的另一家公司。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah. One that comes to mind is definitely Retool. Retool was very different from both my experiences at Stripe and at OpenAI because both Stripe and OpenAI, for better or for worse, were inbound companies, right? There was so much latent demand that we were fighting off people breaking down the door trying to get to our products. With Retool, marketing was between the company and revenue. And we had fantastic product market fit with the enterprise space, with the developer community, but awareness was a challenge. And so how do we go out, not just wait inside of our house waiting for people to knock down the door, but rather step outside of our house and start introducing ourselves to the neighborhood? (00:17:57): So, thinking about outbound channels and building demand engines was the name of the game. And here, one of the ways to think about that is, "Hey, should we just scale the paid marketing channels that we already have working for us?" And that's when the diagnostic really came into play, which is, what are the leads that are coming through the funnel? Are they turning into sales-qualified opportunities? What kind of pipeline are they driving? A lot of marketing metrics, again, tend to be vanity metrics. They tend to be about the number of clicks that you got, number of views that a tweet got, number of impressions. I think those are all bullshit numbers. (00:18:35): Really, what you want to be looking at is your impact on either signups if you're a self-serve product, PLG, or in terms of a B2B company, sales leads and revenue that you're driving, pipeline and opportunity that you're driving. So we diagnosed that and we found that for the most part, our paid social channels were doing not much for us. And so we had to invest in net new engines. So that was the diagnostic. When we looked at some of the competitors, we saw that they were doing a lot of content marketing. They were doing a lot of events programming. And we could've kind of followed in those footsteps, but there was the ability to take a different path. (00:19:13): And so what we decided to do was double down on customer marketing and customer storytelling because the thing that differentiated Retool from a lot of the copycat competitors in the market was that we had terrific traction with true enterprises who were paying for the product, who believed in the product, who were expanding within the product. And so having them tell the stories on our behalf was so much more compelling, and no other company could replicate the kind of customers that Retool had in its bench. So, we wanted to make sure that we were using those logos, we were using those companies to the best impact possible, and then we experimented. We tried to put together webinars, different types of sales dinners, different types of event formats to see what actually worked best for us, and scaled the ones that worked and discarded the ones that didn't.
turns.zh: 是的。我想到的肯定是 Retool。 Retool 与我在 Stripe 和 OpenAI 的经历非常不同，因为无论好坏，Stripe 和 OpenAI 都是入境公司，对吧？潜在需求如此之多，以至于我们不得不阻止那些破门而入试图获得我们产品的人。对于 Retool，营销是在公司和收入之间进行的。我们拥有与企业空间和开发者社区非常契合的产品市场，但意识是一个挑战。那么我们如何出去，不只是在房子里等待人们敲门，而是走出我们的房子，开始向邻居介绍自己呢？ (00:17:57)：所以，思考出站渠道和构建需求引擎就是游戏的名称。在这里，思考这个问题的方法之一是，“嘿，我们是否应该扩大我们已经使用的付费营销渠道？”这就是诊断真正发挥作用的时候，也就是说，通过漏斗的线索是什么？它们是否会转化为符合销售资格的机会？他们正在驾驶什么样的管道？同样，许多营销指标往往都是虚荣指标。它们往往与您获得的点击次数、推文获得的浏览次数、展示次数有关。我认为这些都是胡说八道的数字。 (00:18:35)：实际上，您想要关注的是您对注册的影响（如果您是自助产品、PLG），或者是 B2B 公司、您正在推动的销售线索和收入、您正在推动的渠道和机会。因此，我们对此进行了诊断，发现在大多数情况下，我们的付费社交渠道对我们没有多大作用。因此我们必须投资新的引擎。这就是诊断结果。当我们观察一些竞争对手时，我们发现他们正在进行大量的内容营销。他们做了很多活动编程。我们本来可以追随这些脚步，但我们有能力走不同的道路。 (00:19:13)：因此，我们决定在客户营销和客户故事讲述上加倍努力，因为 Retool 与市场上许多模仿竞争对手的区别在于，我们对真正的企业有巨大的吸引力，他们为产品付费，相信产品，在产品内进行扩张。因此，让他们代表我们讲述故事更具吸引力，没有其他公司可以复制 Retool 的客户类型。因此，我们想确保我们使用这些徽标，我们使用这些公司来发挥最大的影响力，然后我们进行实验。我们尝试将网络研讨会、不同类型的销售晚宴、不同类型的活动形式放在一起，以了解什么实际上最适合我们，并扩大有效的内容并丢弃无效的内容。

There's one more-
turns.zh: 好吧，这里就这么多了。因此，在诊断步骤中，我认为这里的一条言外之意是查看已经起作用的内容。所以你看了看，好吧，也许是付费增长，也许是这个，也许是那个。然后就像是，“好吧，似乎有效的是人们通过另一个标志、另一个很奇特的客户找到我们，他们会说，‘哦，Netflix 正在使用 Retool。哦，也许我应该看看。’”所以我认为这是一个非常重要的教训，不要试图喜欢，“嘿，我们需要开始将我们的漏斗顶部扩展到所有这些不同的渠道。”还有一个——
