turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: You still have to do something a little bit different. I recall a very specific example at Stripe where our product, Stripe Connect, which was made for marketplaces like Uber and Airbnb, where not only are you accepting money as a platform, you're also paying out people on the seller side of the marketplace. The competition truly was to become a payment facilitator. So rather than using another off-the-shelf service, instead of using Stripe Connect, you might go off and become a PayFac yourself. And a lot of the services, organizations, the consulting groups that were helping companies become PayFacs, the things that they were doing was really leaning into that old school terminology, the jargon of the legacy systems and so on and so forth. (00:21:43): And Stripe kind of figured out, "Hey, we need to rank higher for the SEO terms that people are searching for. So how do we help rank for PayFac without actually talking about ourselves as a PayFac solution?" So we decided to kind of do a reverse RFP system where we created a piece of content that said, "Hey, if you want to be a payment facilitator, here's the secret playbook. Here's all the things that you have to do. And by the way, if this feels onerous or annoying, it is, and you should use Stripe Connect instead." So there was still a little bit of a zigging where others were zagging. Yeah, but I think if we had done the same thing in terms of becoming a consulting service to become a payment facilitator, Connect would be nowhere near the sort of run rate or revenue that it drives for the company.
turns.zh: 你仍然需要做一些不同的事情。我记得 Stripe 的一个非常具体的例子，我们的产品 Stripe Connect 是为 Uber 和 Airbnb 等市场制作的，您不仅可以接受金钱作为平台，还可以向市场卖方的人员付款。这场竞赛真正的目的是成为支付服务商。因此，您可以自己成为 PayFac，而不是使用其他现成的服务或 Stripe Connect。许多帮助公司成为 PayFacs 的服务、组织和咨询团体，他们所做的事情实际上都倾向于老式术语、遗留系统的行话等等。 (00:21:43)：Stripe 有点想通了，“嘿，我们需要在人们搜索的 SEO 术语上排名更高。那么，我们如何帮助 PayFac 排名，而不实际谈论我们自己是 PayFac 解决方案呢？”因此，我们决定做一个反向 RFP 系统，我们创建了一段内容，内容是：“嘿，如果你想成为支付服务商，这是秘密手册。这是你必须做的所有事情。顺便说一句，如果这感觉很繁重或烦人，确实如此，你应该使用 Stripe Connect。”因此，在其他人蜿蜒前进的地方，仍然存在一点曲折。是的，但我认为，如果我们在成为咨询服务商和支付服务商方面做同样的事情，Connect 的运行率或收入将远远不及它为公司带来的那种水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And this is a great segue to Stripe, which, another company you were the very first marketing hire at. You were also, I believe, the only marketing person for three years at Stripe.
turns.zh: 好的。这是对 Stripe 的一个很好的延续，你是这家公司第一个营销人员。我相信，您也是 Stripe 三年来唯一的营销人员。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: I do not recommend that to anybody.
turns.zh: 我不向任何人推荐这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lesson there. Okay, so let's talk about Stripe. What are some of the biggest things you learned marketing at Stripe that you think might be helpful to other marketing people and founders?
turns.zh: 那里有一个教训。好吧，我们来谈谈 Stripe。您认为在 Stripe 营销中学到的最重要的东西有哪些可能对其他营销人员和创始人有帮助？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Oh, man, there are so many things to choose from because I was Stripe for almost eight and a half years. Joining as the company's first marketing hire, building that marketing function from the ground up, it really gave me the privilege of working very closely with our founders, John and Patrick. I would say actually I was not the first marketer at Stripe, John and Patrick were the first marketers at Stripe because they were developers themselves. They truly understood the developer community. And when that audience for Stripe was squarely developers to begin with, they knew exactly how to authentically reach that audience. (00:23:24): And so I had to unlearn a lot of the things that I had learned at Google and Dropbox coming into Stripe in order to reach developers authentically. The experience really taught me the importance of deep product understanding as well. You couldn't really play act at understanding the product, especially when developers are trained to spot bugs, right? So not only do they spot those bugs in code, they spot those bugs in marketing and in blog posts. (00:23:51): And so if the marketing pieces are your first impression of the product, they're an extension of the product itself, you have to hold yourself to a very high bar in terms of how you communicate about the product. And so we did a lot of investment in design work, in polish in terms of how the marketing came together. And yeah, the value of creating marketing artifacts that were deeply integrated with the company's mission and the craftsmanship that went into the product was another lesson that I learned very deeply at Stripe.
turns.zh: 哦，伙计，有很多东西可供选择，因为我在 Stripe 工作了将近八年半了。作为公司第一位营销人员加入，从头开始建立营销职能，这确实让我有幸与我们的创始人约翰和帕特里克密切合作。我想说，实际上我并不是 Stripe 的第一个营销人员，John 和 Patrick 是 Stripe 的第一个营销人员，因为他们本身就是开发人员。他们真正了解开发者社区。当 Stripe 的受众一开始就是开发人员时，他们就知道如何真正接触到这些受众。 (00:23:24)：因此，我必须忘掉在 Google 和 Dropbox 中学到的很多东西，进入 Stripe 才能真正接触到开发人员。这次经历也确实教会了我深入了解产品的重要性。你无法真正理解产品，尤其是当开发人员接受过发现错误的培训时，对吗？因此，他们不仅会发现代码中的错误，还会发现营销和博客文章中的错误。 (00:23:51)：因此，如果营销片段是您对产品的第一印象，它们是产品本身的延伸，那么您必须在如何传达产品方面对自己保持很高的标准。因此，我们在设计工作和营销方面进行了大量投资。是的，创造与公司使命和产品工艺深度融合的营销产品的价值是我在 Stripe 学到的另一堂课。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So kind of along those lines, again, people may look at Stripe and be like, "Okay, it's the best thing ever for payments. Why do we need marketing? It's just like, engineers build it and integrate, it works." What is it that marketing most adds to a product like Stripe?
turns.zh: 同样，沿着这些思路，人们可能会看到 Stripe 并说，“好吧，这是有史以来最好的支付方式。为什么我们需要营销？就像工程师构建它并集成它一样，它有效。”像 Stripe 这样的产品，营销最能增加什么？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Across my time at Stripe, marketings are very different purposes. And so I kind of see it in different epochs or chapters of my time at the company. The first chapter when I joined, our head of partnerships at the time, Cristina Cordova, handed me a Hackpad at the time, which is like a notion-
turns.zh: 在我在 Stripe 工作期间，营销的目的非常不同。所以我在公司的不同时期或不同阶段都看到了这一点。我加入的第一章，当时我们的合作伙伴主管克里斯蒂娜·科尔多瓦（Cristina Cordova）当时递给我一个Hackpad，这就像一个概念——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember Hackpad.
turns.zh: 我记得黑客板。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It turned into Dropbox Paper.
turns.zh: 它变成了 Dropbox Paper。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: That's right. And so she had kept a Hackpad, a secret Hackpad away from the engineering team, which was all of the features and products that we had shipped but had never communicated to our customers about. And so the launch sort of ended with shipping the feature rather than communicating with the user. So the first chapter at Stripe was really just getting through that backlog and making sure that the ethos at the company changed to say, "Hey, your launch isn't complete if you're just code complete. You have to actually ship it to the customer and make them aware of it." So usage became the north star, engagement became the north star rather than just the binary, has it launched or not? (00:25:41): The second chapter at Stripe was really starting to expand what a launch meant, right? So, going from just putting out a blog post for people who were already subscribed to the RSS feed of the company versus thinking through, "Hey, how do we reach out to them through an email, through other channels? How do we really invest in this fanatical community that is getting so excited about the product experience?" So we pulled together developer experience as a function, built out developer relations to really have that community feeling and vibe. (00:26:13): And then it was about starting to think through the multi-product ecosystem. So Stripe went from a single-threaded payments processing company to one that had multiple different products and features for the audience and the user base. So then the work of marketing became, how do you help people understand and navigate potentially this multi-product ecosystem and platform to figure out what's the right set of features and solutions that they should be using for their needs?
turns.zh: 这是正确的。因此，她保留了一个 Hackpad，一个远离工程团队的秘密 Hackpad，其中包含我们已交付但从未与客户沟通过的所有功能和产品。因此，发布最终以发布功能而不是与用户沟通而告终。因此，Stripe 的第一章实际上只是处理积压的工作，并确保公司的精神发生变化，“嘿，如果你只是完成代码，那么你的发布还没有完成。你必须将其实际交付给客户并让他们意识到这一点。”因此，使用率成为北极星，参与度成为北极星而不仅仅是双星，它是否已启动？ (00:25:41)：Stripe 的第二章确实开始扩展发布的含义，对吗？因此，从仅仅为已经订阅了公司 RSS 源的人们发布博客文章，到思考“嘿，我们如何通过电子邮件、通过其他渠道联系他们？我们如何真正投资于这个对产品体验如此兴奋的狂热社区？”因此，我们将开发者体验作为一项功能整合在一起，建立了开发者关系，以真正拥有社区的感觉和氛围。 (00:26:13)：然后是开始思考多产品生态系统。因此，Stripe 从一家单线程支付处理公司发展成为一家为受众和用户群提供多种不同产品和功能的公司。那么营销工作就变成了，如何帮助人们理解和驾驭这个多产品生态系统和平台，找出他们应该根据自己的需求使用哪些正确的功能和解决方案？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so this is, again, a good example of marketing can do a lot of different things and depends on the stage, depends on the needs. It almost starts again with diagnose. Where do we have a need for marketing and growth?
turns.zh: 因此，这又是营销可以做很多不同事情的一个很好的例子，并且取决于阶段，取决于需求。诊断几乎又开始了。我们哪里需要营销和增长？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: And especially in hyper-growth companies, I think you have to run that diagnostic every three months, every six months in order to stay adaptable and flexible because those top level goals do change. At some point, we really have to figure out how to scale our sales function. We have to figure out how to scale internationally. And so being adaptable to that meant constant reprioritization and making sure that you were also hiring people who weren't super deep in particular disciplines, but having a team structure that was T-shaped, people who could be flexible to those needs of the company.
turns.zh: 特别是在高速增长的公司中，我认为你必须每三个月、每六个月进行一次诊断，以保持适应性和灵活性，因为这些顶级目标确实会发生变化。在某些时候，我们确实必须弄清楚如何扩展我们的销售职能。我们必须弄清楚如何扩大国际规模。因此，适应这种情况意味着不断重新确定优先顺序，并确保你雇用的人员在特定学科上不是很深入，但拥有 T 形团队结构，可以灵活地满足公司的这些需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to your point about how there's no playbooks, is Stripe another example where it's like, this has never been done before, we shouldn't copy what other payments companies have done in the past?
turns.zh: 回到你关于如何没有剧本的观点，Stripe 是另一个例子吗？以前从未这样做过，我们不应该复制其他支付公司过去所做的事情？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah. If we did, we would still be talking about PCI compliance and payment gateways.
turns.zh: 是的。如果我们这样做，我们仍然会谈论 PCI 合规性和支付网关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so much of what you share that reminds me of Raaz from Wiz, who also, you were an engineer originally, she was a product person. Yeah, I think. I don't know if she was an engineer, but a product person. So it's your-
turns.zh: 你分享的很多内容让我想起了 Wiz 的 Raaz，她也是，你最初是一名工程师，她是一名产品人员。是的，我想。我不知道她是不是工程师，而是产品人员。所以这是你的——

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Her first PM, actually. Yeah, Raaz is great.
turns.zh: 实际上是她的第一任总理。是的，拉兹很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And I think there's a few things that are so interesting here. One is you both have non-marketing backgrounds, you went from another function. And I think, you tell me, it gives you a whole new perspective on marketing, not just the traditional education of marketing. Is there anything there?
turns.zh: 好的。我认为这里有一些事情非常有趣。一是你们都没有营销背景，是从另一个职能部门转过来的。我认为，你告诉我，它给了你一个关于营销的全新视角，而不仅仅是传统的营销教育。那里有什么吗？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: One thing it's definitely made me is very skeptical of most marketing channels and strategies and tactics. And so I would be one of the first people to say, "Is that really going to work? What developer is clicking on paid ads? Isn't a better thing that we could be doing for them telling them to install ad block?" So I think that skepticism means that you just have a higher bar for the quality of the content, the substance of the content. You want to make sure that the marketing is as substantive and as crafted as the product experience itself.
turns.zh: 它确实让我对大多数营销渠道、战略和战术非常怀疑。因此，我会是第一个说“这真的有用吗？哪个开发者点击付费广告？我们可以为他们做的告诉他们安装广告拦截的更好的事情不是更好的事情吗？”所以我认为怀疑意味着你对内容的质量、内容的实质有更高的标准。您需要确保营销与产品体验本身一样实质性和精心设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other really interesting corollary here is she was very big on avoiding the generic acronyms and classic industry norms, I forget what they were, for cloud security. But it's just like, "We're not this thing. We're Wiz. Here's what we do."
turns.zh: 这里另一个非常有趣的推论是，为了云安全，她非常热衷于避免使用通用缩写词和经典行业规范，我忘记它们是什么了。但这就像，“我们不是这个东西。我们是 Wiz。这就是我们所做的。”

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: They are definitely a company that zags when others zig. I still have my Wiz socks, which have these beautiful 8-bit characters on them. Their branding really stands out in the sea of sameness in SaaS conferences.
turns.zh: 他们绝对是一家在其他公司急转直下时也急转直下的公司。我还保留着我的 Wiz 袜子，上面有这些漂亮的 8 位字符。他们的品牌确实在 SaaS 会议的千篇一律的海洋中脱颖而出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. There's something I heard that you did at Stripe that I wanted to ask you about that worked really well. When you came into Stripe, you looked at all of the biggest customer support issues and you turned those into docs to help people serve themselves. Can you just talk about that insight and the power of doing something like that?
turns.zh: 好的。我听说你在 Stripe 做了一些事情，我想问问你，效果非常好。当您进入 Stripe 时，您研究了所有最大的客户支持问题，并将这些问题转化为文档来帮助人们为自己服务。您能谈谈这种洞察力以及做类似事情的力量吗？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah, and this was a great practice that existed at Stripe even before I joined, which is all new hires would do a support rotation just to build empathy with our customers. So, users first was a very core operating principle for the company, and we spent about 20% of our time collectively talking to customers, talking to users, talking to non-users to understand their needs, their gripes about the product. And that tradition, I think, continues to today. The support rotation specifically was such a fantastic fountain of understanding, "Hey, these are the areas that people are confused about." (00:29:54): Again, I kind of mentioned this sort of cheat code of talking to your customers and using the language that they use to describe their problems as a shortcut to fantastic product marketing and messaging, because it really tells you what are their pain points and how can you meet them where they are. You want them nodding their heads along as they're reading your landing pages. And so when I was doing the support rotation, there were thematic things that kept coming up. People were asking, "Hey, do you process subscription payments or recurring payments?" Or, "Can I pay people out with Stripe?" And I was like, "Of course you could, but there's no reason you should know that because we don't tell you anywhere." (00:30:30): And so that ended up being a stacked rank backlog of landing pages that we produce that just educated people. And this is really important when you have strong top of funnel demand, and potentially not as many people and you're not trying to scale your teams linearly. Having those educational resources, especially for developers, a fantastic marketing funnel sometimes doesn't look like talking to sales. It often never looks like talking to sales. It looks like a self-directed educational experience. Even the sales process ends up being very consultative typically with very technical folks on the other side. So yeah, that was a great way and a great program to figure out what content we should focus and prioritize.
turns.zh: 是的，这是在我加入之前 Stripe 就存在的一个很好的做法，即所有新员工都会进行支持轮换，只是为了与我们的客户建立同理心。所以，用户第一是公司非常核心的运营原则，我们花了大约 20% 的时间集体与客户交谈，与用户交谈，与非用户交谈，以了解他们的需求，他们对产品的抱怨。我认为这种传统一直延续到今天。特别是支持轮换是一个非常棒的理解源泉，“嘿，这些是人们感到困惑的领域。” (00:29:54)：我再次提到了这种与客户交谈并使用他们用来描述问题的语言的作弊代码，作为出色的产品营销和消息传递的捷径，因为它确实告诉您他们的痛点是什么以及您如何满足他们的需求。您希望他们在阅读您的着陆页时点头。因此，当我进行支持轮换时，一些主题性的事情不断出现。人们问：“嘿，你们处理订阅付款还是定期付款？”或者，“我可以用 Stripe 向人们付款吗？”我当时想，“你当然可以，但你没有理由知道这一点，因为我们不会在任何地方告诉你。” (00:30:30)：因此，最终我们为受过教育的人制作了一堆积压的登陆页面。当您有强大的漏斗顶部需求，并且可能没有那么多人并且您不尝试线性扩展您的团队时，这一点非常重要。拥有这些教育资源，尤其是对于开发人员而言，出色的营销渠道有时看起来并不像与销售人员交谈。通常看起来不像是在与销售人员交谈。这看起来像是一种自我导向的教育体验。即使是销售过程最终也会与另一方的技术人员进行大量协商。所以，是的，这是一个很好的方法和一个很好的计划，可以确定我们应该关注和优先考虑的内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are really cool just little ways as a new marketing person. You can add value really quickly is kind of what I'm taking away.
turns.zh: 作为一个新的营销人员，这些都是非常酷的小方法。你可以很快地增加价值，这就是我所带走的。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Talking to customers is at the top of the list.
turns.zh: 与客户交谈是首要任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by LinkedIn Ads. One of the hardest and also most important parts of B2B marketing is reaching the right people. I'm constantly getting ads for products that I will never buy, and I almost feel sorry for the money that these companies are spending pitching me on their spend management software or some kind of cybersecurity solution that my one man business just does not need. When you're ready to reach the right professionals, use LinkedIn Ads. LinkedIn has grown to a network of over 1 billion professionals, including 130 million decision makers, and that's where it stands apart from other ad platforms. You can target your ad buyers by job title, industry, company, role, seniority, skills, even company revenue. (00:32:08): All the professionals that you need to reach in one place. Stop wasting budget on the wrong audience and start targeting the right professionals only on LinkedIn Ads. LinkedIn will even give you $100 credit on your next campaign so that you can try it for yourself. Just go to linkedin.com/podlenny. That's linkedin.com/podlenny. Terms and conditions apply. Only on LinkedIn Ads. (00:32:32): There's something else that I know that you're a big advocate of which is internal reviews and just making sure everyone's aligned, which I think a lot of people and especially startups try to avoid. Like, "Let's just move fast. We don't need to have all these meetings where people review stuff," but I know you're a big advocate of that. Talk about why that's so important.
turns.zh: 今天的节目由 LinkedIn Ads 为您带来。 B2B 营销中最困难也是最重要的部分之一就是接触到合适的人。我不断收到我永远不会购买的产品的广告，我几乎为这些公司花很多钱向我推销他们的支出管理软件或某种我的个人业务不需要的网络安全解决方案感到遗憾。当您准备好接触合适的专业人士时，请使用 LinkedIn 广告。 LinkedIn 已发展成为拥有超过 10 亿专业人士（其中包括 1.3 亿决策者）的网络，这就是它与其他广告平台的不同之处。您可以根据职位、行业、公司、角色、资历、技能，甚至公司收入来定位广告买家。 (00:32:08)：您需要在一处联系的所有专业人士。停止将预算浪费在错误的受众身上，并开始仅在 LinkedIn 广告上定位合适的专业人士。 LinkedIn 甚至会在您的下一次活动中为您提供 100 美元的积分，以便您可以亲自尝试。只需访问 linkedin.com/podlenny。那是 linkedin.com/podlenny。条款和条件适用。仅在 LinkedIn 广告上。 (00:32:32)：据我所知，还有一件事是你大力提倡的，那就是内部审查，并确保每个人都保持一致，我认为很多人，尤其是初创公司都试图避免这样做。就像，“让我们快速行动吧。我们不需要召开所有这些会议来让人们审查东西，”但我知道你是这一点的大力倡导者。谈谈为什么这如此重要。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah, this is a hill that I would die on, which is that good process or sufficient process is actually something that speeds up a company rather than slow it down. It stems from this idea that we talked about a little bit, which is that marketing is an extension of your product. It's the first touchpoint your customers have with your product. And ideally, you're setting expectations there in terms of what they should expect once they sign up for the product or commit to a contract and start using it within their companies. And when I think about that, consistency is really, really important. (00:33:20): The other part, the other facet of why process is important is because especially as you're in hyper-growth companies, scaling teams is part and parcel like what you're trying to do. And when you bring in someone new, you want them to be just as self-sufficient as somebody who's been at the company for two years. So in your second week, can you be as successful as someone who's been at the company for two years? And the reason that I have that principle in mind is because it makes you kind of break out of your shell of, "I've been at this company for some time now. I understand the sort of unspoken rules of the organization. I've built up enough social capital that I can withdraw from to get something done. And I know which conference room to stand outside of to get the founder to review a piece of content before it goes out the door." (00:34:09): That is not scalable, that is not sustainable. And so if you want somebody to be successful and contributing member of the organization very, very quickly, setting up some of these processes with the intention of trying to help them navigate how to go from idea to execution can be very empowering and powerful. Nobody wants to do the wrong thing. They want the guardrails to understand what great looks like at the company.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一座我愿意死在上面的山，那就是良好的流程或足够的流程实际上可以加速公司而不是放慢速度。它源于我们刚才谈到的这个想法，即营销是产品的延伸。这是客户与您的产品的第一个接触点。理想情况下，您可以根据他们在注册产品或签订合同并开始在公司内使用该产品后应该期望的内容来设定期望。当我想到这一点时，一致性真的非常非常重要。 (00:33:20)：另一方面，为什么流程很重要的另一个方面是因为特别是当你在高速增长的公司时，扩展团队是你想要做的事情的重要组成部分。当你引进新人时，你希望他们能像在公司工作了两年的人一样自给自足。那么在你的第二周，你能像在公司工作了两年的人一样成功吗？我之所以牢记这一原则，是因为它让你摆脱了自己的束缚，“我在这家公司已经有一段时间了。我了解该组织的潜规则。我已经建立了足够的社会资本，可以退出来完成某件事。而且我知道应该站在哪个会议室外面，让创始人在内容发布之前对其进行审查。” (00:34:09)：这是不可扩展的，也是不可持续的。因此，如果您希望某人非常非常快地取得成功并成为组织的贡献者，那么建立其中一些流程来试图帮助他们了解如何从想法到执行可能会非常有力量和强大。没有人愿意做错事。他们希望护栏了解公司的伟大之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you speak more about what this looks like? Say a startup wants to start implementing something like this.
turns.zh: 您能详细谈谈这是什么样子吗？假设一家初创公司想要开始实施这样的事情。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Two simple processes that you could put into place today is, one, set up a forum called Marketing Review. This can be a live meeting that you host for an hour a week or it can be a Slack channel where people are posting things async, or even an email alias where things get sent to. Have that be transparent to the rest of the organization so anyone in the marketing team, anyone in the product organization can join that forum. What that does is it creates a fishbowl where you see sort of, what are the themes that come out when somebody reviews a piece of content? Are they looking at the strategy? Are they looking at the audience? Are they looking at the words? Are they looking at the sort of design approach? So you learn through osmosis of looking at some of these discussions. (00:35:20): And then I would say don't overdo it. I would say there are probably two checkpoints in a program that are really important to get aligned at. One is the 20% review. A 20% review is a strategy review. What are we trying to accomplish? Who are we trying to do it for, and what is the rough approach that we're going to take? If everyone feels comfortable with that, you come back at the 80% mark where you've done a lot of the work on the artifacts, the different types of teams that have to be involved and how do you take something to market it in the first place. (00:35:49): And the reason that I say 80% is sort of critical because if you come in at the 99% mark and you're just looking for a rubber stamp of approval, and you don't really have the slack in the system to be able to make any changes, then that review was worthless. So come in at the 80% mark where you can still make some substantive changes before it goes out the door. And that serves the purpose of consistency so that your brand is showing up in a consistent way to the audience. And two, it helps the rest of the organization learn from each other.
turns.zh: 您今天可以实施的两个简单流程是，一是建立一个名为“营销评论”的论坛。这可以是您每周主持一小时的实时会议，也可以是人们异步发布内容的 Slack 频道，甚至可以是发送内容的电子邮件别名。让这对组织的其他部分透明，以便营销团队中的任何人、产品组织中的任何人都可以加入该论坛。它的作用是创建一个鱼缸，你可以在其中看到，当有人评论一段内容时会出现什么主题？他们正在考虑战略吗？他们在看观众吗？他们在看文字吗？他们正在考虑哪种设计方法吗？因此，您可以通过观看其中一些讨论来学习。 (00:35:20)：然后我想说不要做得太过分。我想说，程序中可能有两个检查点对于保持一致非常重要。一是20%的评论。 20%的审核是策略审核。我们想要实现什么目标？我们要为谁做这件事，我们将采取什么粗略的方法？如果每个人都对此感到满意，那么您就已经完成了 80% 的工作，您已经在工件、必须参与的不同类型的团队以及首先如何将某些东西推向市场方面做了很多工作。 (00:35:49)：我说 80% 的原因有点关键，因为如果你以 99% 的分数进入，而你只是在寻找批准的橡皮图章，并且你的系统中没有真正的余裕来进行任何更改，那么该审核就毫无价值。因此，在达到 80% 的标准时，您仍然可以在产品退出市场之前进行一些实质性的更改。这有助于保持一致性，以便您的品牌以一致的方式向受众展示。第二，它有助于组织的其他部分相互学习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's almost this unspoken element of what you're describing that I want to dig into a little bit, which is the need and value of having consistent and high quality marketing, communication. Why is that important? There's always this talk of just move fast break things. "We're going to be scrappy. We're not going to be obsessed with perfect quality of our, I don't know, websites and emails." Just, why is that important? Why do you value that? Why should companies maybe value that more?
turns.zh: 你所描述的内容中几乎有一个不言而喻的元素，我想深入探讨一下，这就是拥有一致和高质量的营销、沟通的需求和价值。为什么这很重要？总是有人说只要移动快攻就可以了。 “我们会变得斗志旺盛。我们不会沉迷于我们的网站和电子邮件的完美质量，我不知道。”只是，为什么这么重要？你为什么这么看重？为什么公司应该更看重这一点？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: It's funny because with the companies who value velocity actually do value their brand just as much, but oftentimes they think of these as two siloed separate initiatives that they have to put their headspace and calories towards. And I actually think they are not mutually exclusive. They are actually very interconnected. And so when you understand the consistency of your brand, it actually empowers the organization to move faster because you kind of understand how you want the brand to show up in the world. What is that experience that you want your customers to come away with when they interact with your brand? (00:37:25): And the brand is not just marketing artifacts, it is your product experience. It is how your customer support team talks to them, how they resolve tickets. Are you getting passed between a bunch of different teams or is someone just resolving your ticket right away? It's the experience that they have for candidates when they come to recruit your company. So all of these variety of touch points that touch so many different organizations and teams within your organization, they are the amalgamation that makes up your brand. And so if you think of these two things as separate silos, you are optimizing for entirely the wrong thing.
turns.zh: 这很有趣，因为对于那些重视速度的公司来说，他们实际上也同样重视他们的品牌，但他们常常认为这是两个孤立的独立举措，他们必须将自己的空间和卡路里投入其中。事实上我认为它们并不相互排斥。它们实际上是非常相互关联的。因此，当您了解品牌的一致性时，它实际上使组织能够更快地行动，因为您在某种程度上了解了您希望品牌如何出现在世界上。您希望客户在与您的品牌互动时获得什么样的体验？ (00:37:25)：品牌不仅仅是营销工艺品，更是你的产品体验。这是您的客户支持团队与他们交谈以及解决问题的方式。您是否在一群不同的团队之间被传递，或者是否有人立即解决您的问题？这是他们在招聘您的公司时为候选人提供的经验。因此，所有这些接触点接触到组织内如此多的不同组织和团队，它们构成了您的品牌。因此，如果您将这两件事视为独立的孤岛，那么您正在针对完全错误的事情进行优化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've very viscerally learned the power of brand doing my newsletter. I so fear doing something very wrong in my newsletter. It's like, saying something that's completely off or having something broken, or sending an email by accident to everyone that's not ready. I just feel like once I break that, just there's so much power and trust that people have built for what I share and there's so much power that comes from that trust. If I launch a new podcast, people will assume it will be good if they trust what I do and I maintain high quality. And so it's just like a constant fear I have now of breaking that trust.
turns.zh: 通过我的时事通讯，我深深地体会到了品牌的力量。我非常害怕在我的时事通讯中做一些非常错误的事情。这就像说一些完全不对劲的话或者有什么东西坏了，或者不小心向每个还没有准备好的人发送了一封电子邮件。我只是觉得一旦我打破了这一点，人们就会为我分享的东西建立起如此多的力量和信任，而这种信任就会产生如此多的力量。如果我推出一个新的播客，人们会认为如果他们相信我所做的事情并且我保持高质量，那么它会很好。所以我现在一直担心打破这种信任。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah, I mean whether it's fear that drives you is questionable because I think it's also a commitment to your craft.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是是否是恐惧驱使你是值得怀疑的，因为我认为这也是对你的技艺的承诺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: But I think that's exactly right. A brand is an expectation that you create within your audience.
turns.zh: 但我认为这是完全正确的。品牌是您在受众中创造的期望。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And to what you said, if you have a strong brand that people trust, everything gets easier. You pitch them a new product. Like if Stripes like, "Oh, we have a new billing service." (00:39:08): "Oh. Oh, I bet it'll be awesome because it's Stripe." Or if OpenAI launches something. So it just makes life easier if your brand is strong, if there's trust.
turns.zh: 正如你所说，如果你拥有一个人们信任的强大品牌，一切都会变得更容易。你向他们推销新产品。就像 Stripes 喜欢的那样，“哦，我们有新的计费服务。” (00:39:08)：“哦。哦，我打赌它会很棒，因为它是 Stripe。”或者如果 OpenAI 推出了一些东西。因此，如果你的品牌强大、存在信任，生活就会变得更轻松。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah, and you got to take that responsibility seriously because even with something like Stripe, we know that people are going to come try out things that we put out the door. And so we wanted to make sure that that met up to people's expectations. And same thing with OpenAI. When we launched something, even though we were trying to be first to market and that velocity was so important for the company, oftentimes it also came with sometimes putting the brakes on to kind of understand, how can we improve the quality of the experience? How can we make sure that it is safe? So there were different criteria at the two companies, but a similar ethos overall for the brand experience that we wanted people to experience.
turns.zh: 是的，你必须认真对待这一责任，因为即使有像 Stripe 这样的东西，我们也知道人们会来尝试我们推出的东西。因此，我们希望确保这符合人们的期望。 OpenAI 也是如此。当我们推出某样东西时，尽管我们试图率先进入市场，而且速度对公司来说非常重要，但有时我们也会停下来了解一下，我们如何才能提高体验的质量？我们如何确保它是安全的？因此，两家公司有不同的标准，但我们希望人们体验的品牌体验总体上具有相似的精神。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually come back to OpenAI. How long were they around before you joined? It was like many, many years, right?
turns.zh: 让我们回到OpenAI。在你加入之前他们已经存在多久了？好像很多很多年了，对吧？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Many, many years. So OpenAI had been around for almost a decade as primarily a research organization. They had launched ChatGPT about a year before I joined. And so that was the first foray into saying, "Hey, our work is not just announcing research breakthroughs, it is about putting products into the market."
turns.zh: 很多很多年了。 OpenAI 作为一个主要的研究组织已经存在了近十年。在我加入之前大约一年，他们就推出了 ChatGPT。因此，这是第一次尝试说：“嘿，我们的工作不仅仅是宣布研究突破，而是将产品推向市场。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's a few questions I want to ask here. When is a time to bring in a Krithika? When is it like, "Okay, we need help here"? Or, "A bunch of smart people doing great work, people have the product, but I think we need a marketing person that knows what they're doing."
turns.zh: 所以我想在这里问几个问题。什么时候适合引入 Krithika？什么时候会出现“好吧，我们需要帮助”？或者，“一群聪明的人做得很好，人们拥​​有产品，但我认为我们需要一个知道自己在做什么的营销人员。”

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: I think the first criteria is having tremendous product market fit, which is really important because you're throwing fuel on the fire, and you might be throwing different types of fuel on your particular fire. So one pillar for marketing that you have to think about is product marketing. So, if you have a high velocity engineering organization and product organization that is putting out a lot of different features and your customers aren't able to keep track, maybe the engagement's not so high for some of the newer features versus some of the core features that you had in the past, a product marketer can really help bring a discipline of launch excellence and customer engagement, differentiation in the market. How are you positioning the product? (00:41:15): The second pillar for me is demand generation. So if you have much more of a sales driven buyer journey in motion, how are you bringing the demand engines to bear so that your lead generation, your pipeline generation is staying really strong and solid? Or you might want to think about brand, right? You might want to think about community development as a big part of what you're doing as a company. So it really depends, but I think in all of these, you found a spark of product market fit before you're really going for it. (00:41:43): The second for me is that you're distinguishing enough between capital and marketing and lowercase and marketing. And there's an important distinction I've learned over the years, which is capital and marketing, the marketing team, the marketing function at the company is responsible for those channels and artifacts and engines that are driving the funnel for the company, but they are not the end all be all of the discipline of marketing. (00:42:08): And that's where the lowercase and marketing comes in, which is, what do you stand for as a company? What is the storyline that you're telling as a founder when you're talking to the press, to the larger business community? And then it really is a whole company motion where the product team is thinking about, "How are we going to market? What are we going to market with?" The sales team is figuring out, "What is the right ICP, the right customer profile that decision makers, that we need to be reaching?" And then it is this entire joining of the organizations to make that happen really effectively.
turns.zh: 我认为第一个标准是拥有巨大的产品市场契合度，这非常重要，因为你是在火上浇油，而且你可能会在你的特定火上投入不同类型的燃料。因此，您必须考虑的营销支柱之一是产品营销。因此，如果您有一个高速的工程组织和产品组织，正在推出许多不同的功能，而您的客户无法跟踪，也许某些新功能的参与度与您过去拥有的某些核心功能相比并不那么高，那么产品营销人员确实可以帮助带来卓越的发布和客户参与以及市场差异化的纪律。您如何定位产品？ (00:41:15)：对我来说第二个支柱是需求创造。因此，如果您有更多由销售驱动的买家旅程，您如何利用需求引擎，使您的潜在客户一代、渠道一代保持真正强大和稳固？或者您可能想考虑品牌，对吧？您可能希望将社区发展视为公司所做工作的重要组成部分。所以这确实取决于情况，但我认为在所有这些中，你在真正投入之前就发现了产品市场契合的火花。 (00:41:43)：对我来说第二个是你对资本和营销以及小写和营销之间的区别足够明显。多年来我学到了一个重要的区别，那就是资本和营销、营销团队、公司的营销职能负责那些推动公司漏斗的渠道、工件和引擎，但它们并不是营销学科的最终目标。 (00:42:08)：这就是小写字母和营销的用武之地，也就是说，作为一家公司，你代表什么？作为创始人，当您与媒体和更大的商业界交谈时，您讲述的故事情节是什么？然后，这确实是整个公司的动议，产品团队正在思考：“我们将如何营销？我们将用什么来营销？”销售团队正在弄清楚，“我们需要向决策者传达的正确的 ICP、正确的客户档案是什么？”然后正是组织的整体联合才能真正有效地实现这一目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think along these lines, there's a reason Brian at Airbnb merged marketing, or product marketing and product management. However much of that actually happened or not, but the intention-
turns.zh: 是的。我认为，按照这些思路，Brian 在 Airbnb 合并营销或产品营销和产品管理是有原因的。不管其中大部分是否真的发生了，但其意图——

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: I would be so curious to see a follow-up a few years on on how that's been going.
turns.zh: 我很想看到几年后的后续进展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay, let's have Brian back to talk about that. That'd be really interesting. I wanted to actually ask, an interesting thing is happening with ChatGPT versus Claude, and it's so interesting. Claude is arguably better at many things at code, at least at this point. Things are always changing. It seems to be a better writer in a lot of ways. People prefer it for writing, but it's just like ChatGPT is just dominating. It's like, that's what people associate with AI now is just ChatGPT. It's just caught mindshare globally. What is it, do you think, that allowed ChatGPT just to be that? Is it just first mover advantage? Is it some kind of other element? Has it been better longer? Something really interesting is going on there.
turns.zh: 是的。好吧，让布莱恩回来谈谈这个问题。那真的很有趣。我其实想问的是，ChatGPT 与 Claude 之间发生了一件有趣的事情，而且非常有趣。可以说，克劳德在代码方面的很多方面都做得更好，至少在这一点上是这样。事情总是在变化。从很多方面来看，它似乎是一个更好的作家。人们更喜欢用它来写作，但这就像 ChatGPT 占据主导地位一样。就好像，人们现在与 AI 的联系就是 ChatGPT。它刚刚引起了全球的关注。您认为是什么让 ChatGPT 成为这样的？这仅仅是先发优势吗？它是某种其他元素吗？时间长了有好点吗？那里正在发生一些非常有趣的事情。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: One of the things that comes to mind is the orientation when it comes to large language models, and AI in general, is that we're just at the very beginning innings of this whole paradigm shift. And so every single week there is a new breakthrough in AI that comes out from some lab or the other. There's this one-upmanship on point changes and eval numbers and so on and so forth. But I think to customers, the users of the product, the things that make it delightful are the same things that make any product delightful. And there's a sense of loyalty that builds up over time when there is a shorter and smaller delta between your expectations and your reality. (00:44:30): And where those expectations are exceeded, it is accretive to the brand and your loyalty to the product. And where there is a negative delta, that tends to be something that it really detracts. I guess, long story short, what I'm trying to say is that all of these companies have to think in a much more long-term oriented fashion because it's not about a race of the best chatbot and the best outputs. It's about, how does AI become a positive force for humanity? (00:44:58): And so that's going to take a lot of change management and a lot of collaboration between a variety of different organizations rather than just the companies themselves and the product experience itself, because it's going to permeate every aspect of our lives. Our personal lives, our academic lives, our work lives. And so to make that transformation happen, my hope is these companies are not super focused on just their competition and one-upmanship, but rather thinking about the paradigm changes that need to happen for our society at large.
turns.zh: 我想到的一件事是，当涉及大型语言模型和一般人工智能时，我们正处于整个范式转变的最初阶段。因此，每周都会有某个实验室在人工智能方面取得新的突破。在分数变化和评估数字等等方面存在着这种优势。但我认为，对于客户、产品的用户来说，让产品令人愉悦的因素与让任何产品令人愉悦的因素是一样的。当你的期望与现实之间的差距越来越小时，忠诚感就会随着时间的推移而增强。 (00:44:30)：如果超出了这些期望，就会增加品牌和您对产品的忠诚度。如果存在负增量，则往往会真正减损。我想，长话短说，我想说的是，所有这些公司都必须以更长远的方式思考，因为这不是最好的聊天机器人和最好的输出的竞赛。这是关于，人工智能如何成为人类的积极力量？ (00:44:58)：因此，这将需要大量的变革管理和各种不同组织之间的大量协作，而不仅仅是公司本身和产品体验本身，因为它将渗透到我们生活的各个方面。我们的个人生活、学术生活、工作生活。因此，为了实现这一转变，我希望这些公司不要只过度关注竞争和优势，而是要思考整个社会需要发生的范式变革。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It does feel like they are taking that responsibility really seriously, but it is a massive responsibility. Before we leave OpenAI, it feels like it may be the most impactful, important company in the world right now just because they seem to be at the furthest edge of where AI is going. And so it's just such an interesting place to study. So let me ask you this. Just as a person working there, what's something people may not know that's a wonderful, positive element of how open AI works that's just like, "Oh, that's super interesting"? And then, what was maybe a challenge of working at OpenAI?
turns.zh: 确实感觉他们非常认真地对待这一责任，但这是一个巨大的责任。在我们离开 OpenAI 之前，我们感觉它可能是目前世界上最具影响力、最重要的公司，因为它们似乎处于人工智能发展的最前沿。所以这是一个非常有趣的学习场所。那么让我问你这个问题。就像在那里工作的人一样，人们可能不知道什么是开放人工智能如何运作的一个美妙的、积极的元素，就像“哦，那太有趣了”？那么，在 OpenAI 工作可能面临的挑战是什么？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: A surprising thing that surprised me at the company was just the warmth and intellectual curiosity of my peers and leaders at the company. And truly, the sort of commitment to the mission of making artificial intelligence that benefits all of humanity was not just lip service. It was something that was embodied day to day. The sort of questioning that happened, the sort of pressure testing that happened, the rigor with which products were developed, go-to market strategies were developed, was bar none. (00:46:38): And so that's something that I really admired, and it was a privilege to be a part of that organization. I think challenging, of course, is just being at the eye of the storm, right? The eye of the hurricane. So, all eyes are on OpenAI at all times, and I think that is a good thing because of the ramifications of the product. But it also really raised the stakes in terms of how we operated and with what scrutiny, everything that we did was looked at with.
turns.zh: 在公司让我感到惊讶的是公司同事和领导的热情和求知欲。确实，对让人工智能造福全人类这一使命的承诺不仅仅是口头上的承诺。这是每天都在体现的东西。发生的那种质疑，发生的那种压力测试，产品开发的严格程度，制定进入市场的策略，都是前所未有的。 (00:46:38)：这是我真正钦佩的事情，并且很荣幸成为该组织的一员。我认为挑战当然就是处于风暴中心，对吗？飓风眼。因此，所有人的目光始终都集中在 OpenAI 上，我认为这是一件好事，因为该产品的影响深远。但这也确实提高了我们的运营方式和审查方式以及我们所做的一切都受到审查的风险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you recommend that sort of experience for people? Because I imagine work-life balance wasn't great. I imagine there was a lot of stress and worry constantly. Who's the right... When in your career is this a sort of gig to take on versus not?
turns.zh: 您会向人们推荐这种体验吗？因为我认为工作与生活的平衡不太好。我想一直有很大的压力和担忧。谁是对的……在你的职业生涯中，什么时候这是一种可以接受还是不可以接受的工作？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: I'm a big believer of what Claire Hughes Johnson, who was COO at Stripe, used to share with us, which is there is a concept of a work-life blend and sort of making sure that you're working at a company that has three components. I think first and foremost is always people. So, are the people that you're surrounding yourself with ones that push your thinking, who are kind, who are genuinely interesting people to spend your hours with? Because you're spending a vast majority of your time with them. (00:47:54): The second to me is product, right? Do you go to sleep thinking about the product, waking up, wanting to put it into the hands of more people because you know it is going to be good for them or useful to them? I'm not one of those marketers who can pick up any product and market it. I have to have that conviction behind the product itself. (00:48:15): And then third is sort of potential, right? Not just potential for the company to do well, but potential for your discipline to have an impact on the trajectory of the company. And so when you have that kind of potent combination, it can really change your perspective on what's draining, what's energizing. But being very self-aware of what gives you energy is also very helpful to align with the needs of the company, also.
turns.zh: 我非常相信 Stripe 首席运营官克莱尔·休斯·约翰逊 (Claire Hughes Johnson) 曾经与我们分享的内容，那就是工作与生活融合的概念，并确保你在一家由三个组成部分组成的公司工作。我认为首先也是最重要的始终是人。那么，你周围的人是那些能推动你思考的人、善良的人、真正有趣的人吗？因为你大部分时间都和他们在一起。 (00:47:54)：对我来说第二个是产品，对吧？您是否会在入睡时想着该产品，醒来后是否希望将其交到更多人手中，因为您知道它会对他们有好处或有用？我不是那种可以挑选任何产品并进行营销的营销人员。我必须对产品本身有这样的信念。 (00:48:15)：第三是潜力，对吧？不仅有公司表现出色的潜力，而且你的纪律也有可能对公司的发展轨迹产生影响。因此，当你拥有这种有效的组合时，它确实可以改变你对什么是消耗精力、什么是充满活力的看法。但非常清楚自己的能量来源对于​​满足公司的需求也非常有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's shift to talking about Thrive, which is where you work now, and talk about what your role is. And what's interesting, I think, about this role is you get to work now with a bunch of different startups instead of go really deep with one. So share what you do there. And then, what are some things you've learned there so far from a perspective for marketing?
turns.zh: 让我们转向 Thrive，也就是您现在工作的地方，并谈谈您的角色是什么。我认为，这个角色的有趣之处在于，你现在可以与一堆不同的初创公司合作，而不是深入研究一个公司。所以分享一下你在那里做了什么。那么，从营销的角度来看，到目前为止您学到了哪些东西？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah, surprisingly, more people know about Thrive these days than used to even just a few years ago. Thrive's a very unique type of investment company. And sometimes, when I made the leap, people used to ask me, "Oh, was this always in your ambition to make the leap into the investment side of the house?" And I can honestly say it wasn't. But I think being at a firm like Thrive really gives you a very different perspective and it strengthens your ability to be a stronger operator, whether that's in marketing or go-to market or strategic finance, or whatever other pillar within the company there is. (00:49:32): Yeah, Thrive's mission is to be the most meaningful partner to founders. And so there's a lot of high-concentration, high-conviction investments each year. And Thrive is also unique in that it's a network of builders, and so they are really pulling their investment strategies from having been founders themselves. So my role at the company is to help our entire portfolio with all of their marketing needs, so sometimes it means being interim CMO for some portion of time until they find a great leader to fill that seat. Sometimes it means pressure testing their strategy and making sure that their growth targets are ambitious enough. Sometimes it means looking at a Figma file for a landing page that's going out the next day and making sure the words are as good as they can be. (00:50:14): And that variety across a bunch of industries, a bunch of stages of companies, everything from a company that hasn't even been incorporated yet, all the way to Databricks and Stripe and OpenAI when it comes to the types of organizations that we work with. And in the end, the variety of domains can range from consumer to healthcare, to defense, to B2B SaaS, to AI. So it is a variety pack in the best way possible.
turns.zh: 是的，令人惊讶的是，现在了解 Thrive 的人比几年前还要多。 Thrive 是一家非常独特的投资公司。有时，当我实现这一飞跃时，人们常常问我，“哦，这是否一直是你的野心，想要跨越到投资领域？”我可以诚实地说事实并非如此。但我认为在像 Thrive 这样的公司确实会给你一个非常不同的视角，它会增强你成为更强大运营商的能力，无论是在营销、进入市场、战略财务，还是公司内的任何其他支柱方面。 (00:49:32)：是的，Thrive 的使命是成为创始人最有意义的合作伙伴。因此，每年都会有大量高集中度、高信念的投资。 Thrive 的独特之处还在于，它是一个由建设者组成的网络，因此他们真正将自己的投资策略从创始人的身份中拉出来。因此，我在公司的角色是帮助我们的整个投资组合满足他们的所有营销需求，因此有时这意味着在一段时间内担任临时首席营销官，直到他们找到一位出色的领导者来填补该职位。有时，这意味着对他们的战略进行压力测试，并确保他们的增长目标足够雄心勃勃。有时，这意味着查看 Figma 文件以获取第二天发布的登陆页面，并确保文字尽可能好。 (00:50:14)：当谈到我们合作的组织类型时，这种多样性跨越了一系列行业、一系列阶段的公司，从尚未注册的公司，一直到 Databricks、Stripe 和 OpenAI。最后，各种领域可以涵盖从消费者到医疗保健、国防、B2B SaaS 和人工智能。因此，它是尽可能最好的多样化包装。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so what are some things you've learned so far? Because I imagine this is a very different experience. I don't know, especially things that you've changed your mind on even, working with a bunch of companies, early stage versus, what can I say?
turns.zh: 到目前为止，您学到了哪些东西？因为我想这是一次非常不同的经历。我不知道，尤其是那些你甚至改变主意的事情，与很多公司合作，早期阶段与，我能说什么？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: It's a really different method of operating. And so when you're in the leadership role for marketing within a single organization, you have at least a medium term north star in terms of what your teams are trying to drive for the company. And as much context switching as there might be, there is still one company, ideally one product, one buyer journey. That hasn't always been the case, especially with OpenAI and Stripe, but it can span B2C, B2B, B2D. (00:51:27): Thrive is very different in that if you want to be a meaningful partner to the founders, you cannot just jump from 30-minute call to 30-minute call to 30-minute call. You have to go deep to understand the context. And if anything, it's really underscored my ethos that you as a marketer, the best thing that you can bring to the table is your adaptability and flexibility. So, to really diagnose and not just try to spot patterns and themes and playbooks for these companies, but rather be very deep in the trenches with them to understand their unique context, their unique concerns, their unique characteristics, and their values and what they want to bring into the world. (00:52:05): The reason that they want to work with Thrive is not because we are bringing our past experiences to the table, but rather because they're trying to do something new that has never been done in the world. And so those are engagements that are the most exciting is that you are building and going into uncharted territory alongside these founders.
turns.zh: 这是一种完全不同的操作方法。因此，当您在单个组织内担任营销领导角色时，就您的团队试图为公司推动的目标而言，您至少拥有一个中期北极星。尽管可能有尽可能多的环境切换，但仍然是一家公司，最好是一种产品，一种买家旅程。情况并非总是如此，尤其是 OpenAI 和 Stripe，但它可以跨越 B2C、B2B、B2D。 (00:51:27)：Thrive 非常不同，如果你想成为创始人有意义的合作伙伴，你不能从 30 分钟的通话跳到 30 分钟的通话，再到 30 分钟的通话。你必须深入了解上下文。如果说有什么不同的话，那就是它确实强调了我的理念，即作为一名营销人员，你能带来的最好的东西就是你的适应能力和灵活性。因此，要真正诊断，而不仅仅是试图发现这些公司的模式、主题和剧本，而是要深入了解他们的独特背景、他们独特的关注点、他们独特的特征、他们的价值观以及他们想给世界带来什么。 (00:52:05)：他们想要与 Thrive 合作的原因不是因为我们将过去的经验带到桌面上，而是因为他们正在尝试做一些世界上从未做过的新事情。因此，最令人兴奋的是，您正在与这些创始人一起构建并进入未知领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I bet they're all like, "Krithika, what is the playbook for growing this B2B SaaS company?" And you're like, "Nope."
turns.zh: 我敢打赌他们都会说，“Krithika，发展这家 B2B SaaS 公司的策略是什么？”你会说：“不。”

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: And I say, "There is none."
turns.zh: 我说：“没有。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Damn. But we got the framework that we talked about. Okay, I want to zoom out a little bit and talk about just career advice for marketing people, whether it's early stage or later stage. You have this concept, the chameleon CMO. Talk about that and why that's important for marketing folks to think about.
turns.zh: 该死。但我们得到了我们谈论的框架。好吧，我想把范围缩小一点，谈谈对营销人员的职业建议，无论是早期阶段还是后期阶段。你有这个概念，变色龙 CMO。谈谈这一点以及为什么这对营销人员来说很重要。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah. The conventional wisdom for many CMOs is to be like a T-shaped marketer. And what that means is go deep in one of these pillars that we talked about, product marketing, demand marketing, brand marketing, and that kind of becomes your calling card in the world. If a company needs brand expertise, they go for this kind of flavor of CMO. Or if a company needs to really grow their pipeline or their demand gen or their consumer growth, they go for more of a demand and growth-oriented CMO. And I think this chameleon CMO concept is a bit of a novel one in that, again, I think modern marketing leaders have to be really good at a bunch of different things. (00:53:30): They have to be very analytical. They have to be best friends with the data science pod because they need to understand the impact of their marketing. They, of course, have to bring creativity, but it is in service to the buyer journey. It is in service to revenue goals and goals that they share with the sales team or the product team and so on, so marketing operating in a silo is no longer a real possibility. So the ability to diversify your interest, maybe going from T-shaped to comb-shaped is probably the right approach here so that you can go deeper in different domains when it is useful for the company through the diagnostic that you do.
turns.zh: 是的。许多 CMO 的传统观念是像 T 型营销人员一样。这意味着深入我们谈到的这些支柱之一，产品营销、需求营销、品牌营销，而这将成为你在世界上的名片。如果一家公司需要品牌专业知识，他们就会选择这种风格的 CMO。或者，如果一家公司需要真正扩大其管道、需求生成或消费者增长，他们会选择更多以需求和增长为导向的 CMO。我认为这种变色龙 CMO 概念有点新颖，因为我认为现代营销领导者必须真正擅长一堆不同的事情。 (00:53:30)：他们必须非常善于分析。他们必须成为数据科学小组最好的朋友，因为他们需要了解营销的影响。当然，他们必须带来创造力，但它是为买家旅程服务的。它服务于收入目标以及他们与销售团队或产品团队等共享的目标，因此在筒仓中进行营销不再是真正的可能性。因此，能够使你的兴趣多样化，也许从 T 形到梳子形可能是正确的方法，这样当通过你所做的诊断对公司有用时，你就可以更深入地研究不同的领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds very hard. I love this beneficial of the comb shape. It sounds like I have so much to learn, so many little skills to build.
turns.zh: 这听起来很难。我喜欢这种有益的梳子形状。听起来我有很多东西要学，有很多小技能需要培养。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Before AI can come in handy. Some of the most brand marketers can become very analytical with the support of a tool like ChatGPT. If your eyes glaze over when you look at giant dumps of CSVs, it's nice to have a partner that is nonjudgmental to kind of push your thinking and to help you understand the details of the data behind the brand work that you might be doing, or vice versa. If you're a very creative product marketer, a very analytical growth marketer, you can work with ChatGPT to be more of a brainstorm partner and really push your thinking on the creative side. So I think becoming a non T-shaped marketer is getting a little bit easier.
turns.zh: 在人工智能派上用场之前。在 ChatGPT 等工具的支持下，一些最有品牌的营销人员可以变得非常善于分析。如果您在看到大量 CSV 时目光呆滞，那么很高兴有一个不带偏见的合作伙伴来推动您的思考并帮助您了解您可能正在做的品牌工作背后的数据细节，反之亦然。如果您是一位非常有创意的产品营销人员，一位非常善于分析的增长营销人员，那么您可以与 ChatGPT 合作，成为更多的头脑风暴合作伙伴，并真正推动您的创意方面的思考。所以我认为成为一个非T型营销人员变得更容易了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point. A good segue to an AI question. Hey, we got to talk about AI. One of your former colleagues, Kevin Garcia, wanted me to ask you something. He suggested I ask you about taste and creativity in AI. So he said that you're one of the best writers that he's ever worked with. You combine technical backgrounds with creative taste. You do pottery, you should. And you're a voracious reader. And he wanted just to poke at what you think about just how taste and creativity and writing change in the era of AI.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的观点。很好地解决了人工智能问题。嘿，我们得谈谈人工智能。你的一位前同事凯文·加西亚 (Kevin Garcia) 要我问你一件事。他建议我问你有关人工智能的品味和创造力的问题。所以他说你是他合作过的最好的作家之一。您将技术背景与创意品味结合起来。你会做陶艺，你应该这样做。你是一个贪婪的读者。他只是想探究一下你对人工智能时代品味、创造力和写作如何变化的看法。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: I think it's going to become so much more important. First of all, I will say I am not a ChatGPT hyphen person. I was an em dasher well before it became a ChatGPT thing.
turns.zh: 我认为它会变得更加重要。首先，我要说我不是一个 ChatGPT 连字符人。在 Em dasher 成为 ChatGPT 之前我就已经是一名 em dasher 了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Me too. Me too. I hate that. But just for people don't know, people are filtering out em dashes, right? Because they think ChatGPT is the only thing using em dashes?
turns.zh: 我也是。我也是。我讨厌那样。但只是人们不知道，人们正在过滤破折号，对吗？因为他们认为 ChatGPT 是唯一使用破折号的东西？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah, and I don't know what to do about it because this is such a core part of my identity, but-
turns.zh: 是的，我不知道该怎么办，因为这是我身份的核心部分，但是-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a big statement, the em dash.
turns.zh: 这是一个很大的声明，破折号。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: To take a step back though, I think if anything, taste is going to become a distinguishing factor in the age of AI because there's going to be so much drivel that is generated by AI, can be generated by AI, that power is at anyone's fingertips. But truly, the companies that are going to distinguish themselves are the ones that show their craft. That they show their true understanding of the product, the true understanding of their customer, and connect the two in meaningful ways. If they can use AI to augment their efforts to make that happen, that's better than them subsuming their efforts. So to build taste, there's plenty of past episodes that you yourself have recorded that get into building that work. But to me, that is going to be a real differentiator for not only great marketers but great companies to stand out in the field.
turns.zh: 不过，退一步说，我认为，如果说有什么不同的话，那就是品味将成为人工智能时代的一个显着因素，因为人工智能会产生大量胡言乱语，人工智能也可能产生这种胡言乱语，这种力量触手可及。但事实上，那些能够脱颖而出的公司是那些展示自己技术的公司。他们表现出对产品的真正理解，对客户的真正理解，并以有意义的方式将两者联系起来。如果他们可以使用人工智能来增强他们的努力以实现这一目标，那就比他们将自己的努力纳入其中更好。因此，为了培养品味，你自己录制了很多过去的剧集来构建这部作品。但对我来说，这不仅对于伟大的营销人员而且对于伟大的公司来说都将成为在该领域脱颖而出的真正差异化因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a concept that I love that recently I learned from Guillermo at Vercel. He calls it exposure hours. That's when I asked him how to build taste, and that's kind of a value they have at their company is just increase your exposure hours to great stuff, because that is how you build taste. I love that. It's such a simple actionable thing you can do.
turns.zh: 我最近从 Vercel 的 Guillermo 那里学到了一个我喜欢的概念。他称之为曝光时间。就在那时，我问他如何培养品味，他们公司的一种价值就是增加你接触优秀事物的时间，因为这就是你培养品味的方式。我喜欢那个。这是您可以做的简单可行的事情。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: And at Thrive, we have this share channel, which is just sharing things that we're seeing out into the world. It's not particularly deal flow news or competitive news or anything like that, but it is things that we have seen that resonated with us for whatever reason.
turns.zh: 在 Thrive，我们有这个分享渠道，它只是分享我们在世界上看到的东西。这并不是特别的交易流新闻或竞争新闻或类似的新闻，而是我们所看到的、无论出于何种原因引起我们共鸣的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines of not over-relying on ChatGPT, AI tools for writing and creativity, it feels like there's going to be a big issue with people just starting early in their career where they just never learn how to do the thing, and they just rely really heavily on ChatGPT and tools like that to write, to email, to communicate well. I guess, do you have any advice for folks that are early career, just how to find that balance of not over-relying but still leveraging these tools?
turns.zh: 沿着不过度依赖ChatGPT这种用于写作和创造力的人工智能工具的思路，对于刚刚开始职业生涯的人们来说，这感觉会是一个大问题，他们永远不会学习如何做这件事，他们只是严重依赖ChatGPT和类似的工具来写作、发送电子邮件和进行良好的沟通。我想，您对职业生涯早期的人有什么建议吗？如何找到不过度依赖但仍然利用这些工具的平衡？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: I think there's two schools of thought here. One is that sort of the domain, the discipline itself stays static and the way that you approach it changes over time, whether you're going at it in a manual way or an automated way or an AI augmented way. But I think the other school of thought, which I more believe in, is that the discipline itself is changing. And so what it means to market a product, what it means to show up as a fantastic operator is in and itself changing. So if you're not leveraging some of these tools, you will be putting yourself at a disadvantage. But understanding the underlying mechanics, this is why I would still be a very firm believer in STEM education, is that you understand the fundamental concepts. And then you can have a choice and optionality in how you decide to apply those concepts, but the concepts themselves have to be there in the foundations.
turns.zh: 我认为这里有两种思想流派。一是这样的领域，学科本身保持静态，而你处理它的方式会随着时间的推移而变化，无论你是以手动方式、自动化方式还是人工智能增强方式。但我认为我更相信的另一种思想流派是学科本身正在发生变化。因此，营销产品的意义、展现优秀运营商的意义本身就在发生变化。因此，如果您不利用其中一些工具，您将使自己处于不利地位。但了解其基本原理，这就是为什么我仍然坚定地相信 STEM 教育，因为你了解基本概念。然后你可以选择如何应用这些概念，但概念本身必须存在于基础中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Easier said than done because there's all these tools now and you're just like, "Hey, I need to write a report for school. I guess I could just, maybe this time I'll just ask ChatGPT to help me with this one."
turns.zh: 是的。说起来容易做起来难，因为现在有了所有这些工具，您就像，“嘿，我需要为学校写一份报告。我想我可以，也许这次我会要求 ChatGPT 帮助我完成这个报告。”

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Yeah, the mindset of learning has to be maybe the one that we have to really imbue as a value. Because being of that growth mindset, if you go to school just to earn the grades or to finish the coursework, it's a very different mindset than if you go to school to learn those concepts and to understand how to apply them.
turns.zh: 是的，学习的心态也许必须成为我们必须真正灌输的一种价值观。因为具有成长心态，如果你去学校只是为了获得成绩或完成课程作业，那么这与你去学校学习这些概念并了解如何应用它们的心态非常不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's something that stuck with me from my chat with Toby Lutke from Shopify. We were chatting about just what is the most important things to incubate in your child? And his answer I loved, which is just, "Curiosity."
turns.zh: 在我与 Shopify 的 Toby Lutke 的聊天中，这一点一直让我印象深刻。我们正在讨论对您的孩子来说最重要的事情是什么？我喜欢他的回答，那就是“好奇心”。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and that's what you're kind of speaking to is just if you're curious about learning, you'll almost avoid some of these things or you'll use these tools in a really interesting way just to learn things more deeply.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是你所说的，如果你对学习感到好奇，你几乎会避免其中的一些事情，或者你会以一种非常有趣的方式使用这些工具，只是为了更深入地学习东西。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: And that stays with you into your career, right? Because you can either go into your career trying to get to that next ladder in the promotion rung or you can get there to bring a genuine curiosity to, what makes us different? What makes our customers tick? And how do we find those unique insights that can unlock something that nobody else has?
turns.zh: 这会伴随你的职业生涯，对吗？因为您可以在进入职业生涯时尝试进入晋升阶段的下一个阶梯，也可以带着真正的好奇心来了解我们的与众不同之处？是什么让我们的客户满意？我们如何找到那些独特的见解来解锁其他人没有的东西？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me. To sort of close out our conversation, I wanted to come back to pricing strategy. I have that in my notes here and I haven't gone back to it. So let's focus on the AI and pricing strategy. Just say someone is trying to figure out pricing for their product and they have some kind of AI product. What are some tips, some piece of advice to think this through? Any general frameworks you use?
turns.zh: 这让我想起了。为了结束我们的谈话，我想回到定价策略。我在我的笔记中记下了这一点，但我没有再回头看它。因此，让我们关注人工智能和定价策略。假设有人正在尝试计算其产品的定价，并且他们有某种人工智能产品。有哪些技巧和建议可以帮助您思考这个问题？您使用任何通用框架吗？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Again, there's no playbook. I feel like it's such a non-answer, but I think the real answer is experimentation. And we found this firsthand multiple times at Stripe, but also at Retool. I think there was a very visceral example where we decided to bring our free product into the hands of more users and sort of what was available in the free plan. And then there was another one that we tested out as a pricing function where we decided to do something quite controversial, which is to take the thing that our sales team was gated on, a self-hosted version of Retool, and made that available self-serve to anybody who wanted it. They didn't have to talk to a salesperson. And that kind of blew up the funnel, right? Because the amount of pipeline that the sales team saw had diminished considerably, but it also helped them focus up market, on higher ACV deals. (01:01:13): And so that trade-off is really hard to make, so the only way we could do it was through experimentation and piloting to build conviction. So I would say AI is no different in that you kind of have to test the market to see what works. Is it a seed-based model? Is that where people are deriving value? Or is the way that they speak about the value of the product something quite different? Is it hours saved? Is it the amount of things that they could do now that they couldn't do before? And so there might be a metric there to go off of, and I don't think anyone solved it, especially with agents coming into play. How you pay for AI workers is going to be very different. What is that unit of completion for things like code generators? It's going to be a Wild, Wild West before we come up with something that is as internalized now as seed-based pricing or usage-based pricing.
turns.zh: 再说一次，没有剧本。我觉得这不是答案，但我认为真正的答案是实验。我们在 Stripe 和 Retool 上多次亲眼目睹了这一点。我认为有一个非常深刻的例子，我们决定将我们的免费产品带到更多用户手中，以及免费计划中提供的内容。然后，我们测试了另一个作为定价功能的功能，我们决定做一些颇具争议的事情，即采用我们的销售团队所控制的东西，即 Retool 的自托管版本，并向任何需要它的人提供自助服务。他们不必与销售人员交谈。这有点炸毁了漏斗，对吧？因为销售团队看到的管道数量大幅减少，但这也帮助他们专注于更高的 ACV 交易市场。 (01:01:13)：因此，这种权衡确实很难做出，所以我们能做到这一点的唯一方法是通过实验和试点来建立信念。所以我想说人工智能没有什么不同，因为你必须测试市场才能知道什么是有效的。它是基于种子的模型吗？这是人们获取价值的地方吗？或者他们谈论产品价值的方式完全不同吗？节省了几个小时吗？是他们现在能做的事情数量是以前做不到的吗？因此，可能存在一个衡量标准，但我认为没有人解决这个问题，尤其是在代理发挥作用的情况下。为人工智能员工支付报酬的方式将会非常不同。代码生成器之类的完成单位是什么？在我们想出像基于种子的定价或基于使用的定价这样内化的东西之前，这将是一个狂野的西部。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wild indeed. I want to actually follow this insight you had around Retool. That's really interesting. Yeah, so you opened up self-hosted Retool. What was the insight there, because this might be useful to people, that convinced you to play with that? Seems like a big deal change to how you price and do trials.
turns.zh: 确实很狂野。我想真正遵循您对 Retool 的见解。这真的很有趣。是的，所以你打开了自托管的 Retool。那里的洞察是什么，因为这可能对人们有用，说服你去玩它？定价和试验方式似乎发生了重大变化。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: There were two guiding principles here. One is, do people actually want to talk to sales before they get a self-hosted thing? It's sort of like the SSO attacks, right? Is that really the thing that you want to gate your value on? So, that was one. And so we saw a lot of demand from smaller customers that still wanted self-hosted for a variety of reasons, because they worked in regulated industries or they worked with very private data and PII. And so it wasn't just something that was, "Hey, if you have 10,000 employees at your company and you're an enterprise, you want self-hosted." It was that for a variety of different reasons, regardless of your company size, you might want self-hosted. So that insight kind of led us to say, "Hey, where is the delineation here? Because the sales team should be talking to larger customers, landing larger deals." And so to align those two was one of the driving principles.
turns.zh: 这里有两个指导原则。一是，人们在获得自托管产品之前真的想与销售人员交谈吗？这有点像 SSO 攻击，对吧？这真的是你想要衡量自己价值的东西吗？所以，这就是其中之一。因此，我们看到小型客户的大量需求，他们出于各种原因仍然希望自行托管，因为他们在受监管的行业工作，或者他们使用非常私人的数据和 PII。因此，这不仅仅是“嘿，如果您的公司有 10,000 名员工，并且您是一家企业，那么您需要自我托管。”出于各种不同的原因，无论您的公司规模如何，您可能都需要自托管。因此，这种洞察力让我们说：“嘿，这里的界限在哪里？因为销售团队应该与更大的客户交谈，达成更大的交易。”因此，将两者结合起来是驱动原则之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Two final questions before we get to our very exciting lighting around. I'm going to take you to a couple of recurring segments on this podcast. The first is AI Corner. And with AI Corner, what I try to get to is some way that you have figured out to use an AI tool in your work to do better work or do faster work, to be more efficient. Is there something there that you could share? And if not, that's also totally cool.
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。在我们开始讨论令人兴奋的灯光之前，还有最后两个问题。我将带您观看此播客中的几个重复出现的片段。第一个是AI角。通过人工智能角，我试图找到的是你在工作中使用人工智能工具来更好地完成工作或更快地完成工作、提高效率的某种方式。有什么可以分享的吗？如果没有，那也很酷。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: Ooh, it is hard to pick because there's not many things I don't use AI for these days, and oftentimes it's a catalyst and an accelerant to the work that I'm already doing. But I think I can actually unlock my ability to talk to dozens of companies across the Thrive portfolio in any given week, and the ability to get deep on their context, their environment, their competitive landscape. We can do that because of the tools and the products that Thrive has invested in from an engineering perspective. So we have internal tools that are driven with AI that give us a lot of insights and access to expertise for these companies so we can show up as more meaningful partners in a day-to-day basis. (01:04:29): So I think the ability to mix AI tooling then accelerates work that you're already doing, and then AI-based tools that unlock superpowers that wouldn't otherwise be available to you unless you're going deep into Google Groups archives or talking to people across the organization to pull out things that are inside of their brain. That kind of institutional knowledge being made more accessible by AI is actually more powerful sometimes than the tools themselves. And in fact, even at OpenAI, it's one of the things that we advised most enterprises to invest in first is their own operational efficiency rather than just the AI magic dust they could sprinkle on top of their product experience for their customers.
turns.zh: 哦，很难做出选择，因为这些天我没有多少事情不使用人工智能，而且通常它是我已经在做的工作的催化剂和促进剂。但我认为我实际上可以在任何一周内与 Thrive 投资组合中的数十家公司进行交谈，并深入了解他们的背景、环境和竞争格局。我们之所以能够做到这一点，是因为 Thrive 从工程角度投资了工具和产品。因此，我们拥有由人工智能驱动的内部工具，可以为我们提供大量见解并获得这些公司的专业知识，这样我们就可以在日常工作中成为更有意义的合作伙伴。 (01:04:29)：所以我认为混合人工智能工具的能力可以加速你已经在做的工作，然后基于人工智能的工具可以解锁你无法获得的超能力，除非你深入谷歌网上论坛档案或与整个组织的人员交谈以提取他们大脑中的东西。人工智能使这种机构知识变得更容易获取，有时实际上比工具本身更强大。事实上，即使在 OpenAI，我们建议大多数企业首先投资的事情之一就是他们自己的运营效率，而不仅仅是他们可以为客户的产品体验撒上 AI 魔法粉末。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Final segment of the podcast we call Fail Corner. And the idea here is we have all these amazing guests, all these super successful people on the podcast, all these stories of epic wins and nothing but success. And I think in reality, that's not the case. And it's important for people to hear that things aren't always up and to the right and always win, win, win. Is there a story from your career you can share where things didn't work out and what you learned from that experience?
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。播客的最后一部分我们称之为“失败角”。这里的想法是，我们拥有所有这些令人惊叹的嘉宾，播客中所有这些超级成功的人，所有这些史诗般的胜利故事，除了成功之外什么也没有。我认为现实情况并非如此。对于人们来说，重要的是要听到事情并不总是向好的方向发展，并且总是赢、赢、赢。在您的职业生涯中，是否有一个故事可以分享，其中哪些事情没有成功，以及您从这次经历中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: And again, this question's hard because there's so many things to choose from as potential examples here. And you're absolutely right, Lenny, in that most careers are not the sort of linear journeys that are reflected on somebody's LinkedIn profile. No, I'll talk about a fantastic success, which is called Stripe Relay, which you probably... Oh, I'm just kidding because nobody remembers it. It was ahead of its market. We launched it back in 2014. It was supposed to be the platform with which e-commerce companies would tap into social commerce. The buy buttons if you remember that. And it launched to a lot of fanfare, but then eventually failed. It didn't produce the sort of revenue or the numbers that we had expected. (01:06:28): And the understanding here was that as much as one side of the marketplace, or you might have some conviction that you need to put something into the market for a particular moment in time, the timing of the market really matters. And the timing of multiple parties coming together to make a platform work really matters. And so the learning here was we hadn't gone deep enough into the market dynamics. We hadn't done enough user research. Did people really want this? And if they did, what were their alternatives? What was the stacks that they were operating in? And would they adopt a net new tool versus one that integrated into existing systems directly like their e-commerce inventory management systems and so on? And so for that reason, I think, again, it was ahead of its market and ahead of its time, but a clear flop regardless of the effort that we put into that launch.
turns.zh: 再说一遍，这个问题很难，因为这里有很多东西可供选择作为潜在的例子。莱尼，你说得完全正确，大多数职业都不是某人 LinkedIn 个人资料中反映的那种线性旅程。不，我会谈论一个巨大的成功，它被称为 Stripe Relay，你可能......哦，我只是在开玩笑，因为没有人记得它。它领先于市场。我们早在 2014 年就推出了它。它本来应该是电子商务公司进军社交商务的平台。如果你还记得的话，就是购买按钮。它一推出就引起了很大的轰动，但最终失败了。它没有产生我们预期的收入或数字。 (01:06:28)：这里的理解是，尽管市场的一方面，或者您可能坚信您需要在特定时刻将某些东西投入市场，但市场的时机确实很重要。多方齐心协力使平台发挥作用的时机确实很重要。因此，我们学到的教训是，我们对市场动态的了解还不够深入。我们没有做足够的用户研究。人们真的想要这个吗？如果他们这样做了，他们的选择是什么？他们操作的堆栈是什么？他们是否会采用一种全新的工具，而不是直接集成到现有系统（如电子商务库存管理系统等）中的工具？因此，出于这个原因，我认为，它再次领先于市场和时代，但无论我们为该发布付出多少努力，它都明显失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of when Kevin Weil was on the podcast talking about Libra, which was his cryptocurrency project that Facebook ran, and he's just like, "Okay, that was a terrible time to launch something like that where people trusted Facebook the least in our history." And now may be a good time to try something like that. Basically, a cryptocurrency platform to send money internationally for free. What a dream that would be. Okay. Krithika, is there anything else you wanted to share or maybe something you wanted to remind people of from what we've talked about? Just to leave folks with a final nugget before we get to our very exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 这让我想起凯文·韦尔 (Kevin Weil) 在播客上谈论 Libra 时，这是 Facebook 运行的他的加密货币项目，他只是说，“好吧，那是推出这样的东西的糟糕时机，人们在我们历史上最不信任 Facebook。”现在可能是尝试类似事情的好时机。基本上，这是一个免费国际汇款的加密货币平台。那将是多么美好的梦想啊。好的。 Krithika，您还有什么想分享的吗？或者您想从我们谈论的内容中提醒人们什么？只是为了在我们进入非常激动人心的闪电回合之前给大家留下最后的金块。

turns.speaker: Krithika Shankarraman
turns.en: If there's one thing that folks take away, I hope it is that they know that there isn't one clear answer to any of the marketing problems. It seems like there's a playbook for everything, there is a framework for everything, but the reality is the work is hard. You have to spend the hours and the time to really understand your customer, and there is no replacement for that, and there isn't going to be even with the advent of AI. And the other part of it is to deeply understand your product as well. What are you bringing to the table? And not just your product, but your company's values, your unique approach that you're bringing to the table. And really be intentional and thoughtful about that because in the absence of that, nothing is going to be a substitute to bring that combination of ingredients together.
turns.zh: 如果人们要带走一件事，我希望他们知道，任何营销问题都没有一个明确的答案。似乎一切都有一个剧本，一切都有一个框架，但现实是工作很困难。你必须花费大量的时间和时间来真正了解你的客户，这是无可替代的，即使人工智能的出现也不会替代。另一部分是深入了解您的产品。你要带来什么？不仅仅是您的产品，还有您公司的价值观以及您所提出的独特方法。对此要真正有意识和深思熟虑，因为如果没有这一点，没有什么可以替代将这些成分组合在一起。
